Given a finite harmonic morphism $f: X \to Y$ between tropical curves and a rational function $p \in k(X)$, we use $f$ to define a pull-back of the rational function semifield $k(X)$, denoted as $f_*: k(X) \to k(Y)$. This operation respects equality and addsitively, making $f_*: k(X) \to k(Y)$ a homomorphism of semifields. Furthermore, $f_*$ is injective and facilitates a description of the Picard variety $\text{Pic}(X)$ in terms of $\text{Pic}(Y)$ and the ramification locus of $f$. Building upon this, we explore various geometric and algebraic consequences of $f_*$, including an analysis of the degree map $\text{Deg}: \text{Pic}(X) \to \mathbb{Z}$ and a study of pull-backs of Valuative Tree T -points. Moreover, we establish that the action of pulling back rational functions induces a group action of the semifield automorphisms of $k(X)$ on the set of T -points of the Berkovich space $X^{\text{an}}$, and that this mimics the situation found in A. Baker's work on algebraic curves. Finally, we show that for X and Y being non-complete tropical curves and p being a rational function on X, the image $f_*: k(X) \to k(Y)$ is isomorphic to the pull-back of the semifield of rational functions from X to Y under the canonical map $k(X) \to k(X)$. This latter result generalizes a technique employed in J. Riedl's work on tropical Hurwitz numbers. It also leads to a new way to compute the length of orbits under the action of the algebraic K-group $k(X)_{\text{alg}} \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k$ on $\text{Pic}(X)$, a practice previously demonstrated with specific examples only. It is hoped that this new approach to computing lengths of orbits could be applied more widely. Moreover, it is hoped that a similar pull-back operation for finite separable morphisms between algebraic curves could be defined, one that would make a homomorphism of semifields $f_*: k(X) \to k(Y)$. Using a one-loop effective theory of a single fermion flavour, we examine how the properties of neutron stars and white dwarfs are influenced by their scalar self-coupling. We calculate the scalar condensate's impact on neutron star and white dwarf equations of state, taking into account the influence of this condensate on neutron and electron densities. Our analysis yields three distinct scenario's for the neutron star phase, depending on the self-coupling's strength: in the weakly coupled regime, where neutron star properties remain largely unchanged; in a moderately coupled regime, where neutron star properties are significantly altered, resulting in a massive compact star; and in a highly coupled regime, where neutron stars and white dwarfs merge into a single entity, characterised by a scalar field-driven mass threshold. We demonstrate that a general effective theory of a single flavour can be employed to investigate neutron star phases and deduce the smallest possible neutrino mass state's characteristics. Furthermore, our findings pinpoint the scalar self-coupling's optimal value for stable compact stars and estimate the strength of this coupling. Our study also highlights the need for precise compilations of big Bang nucleosynthesis constraints in conjunction with compact stars' observational data to discern the neutrino mass state's smallest possible value. Lastly, we establish the relationship between this coupling's optimal value and big Bang nucleosynthesis's tightest limits on the neutrino mean square radius. Our research paves the way for a multidimensional effective theory of multiple fermion flavours, enabling a comprehensive understanding of compact stars, big Bang nucleosynthesis, and neutrino properties. The stability of compact stars imposes the most stringent limitation on the smallest possible neutrino mass state, which must exceed half of a specific scalar particle's mass. The findings of this study can be applied to models involving additional scalar fields coupled to neutrinos, and it highlights the significance of big Bang nucleosynthesis's tightest limits on the neutrino mean square radius in such scenarios. The study also forecasts that future research will uncover neutron star phases beyond the one-loop effective theory's scope. The most stable compact stars exist at a self-coupling of approximately $10^{-12}$ (or $10^{-11}$ for the Weyl-like coupling), which is essentially the smallest possible value for the smallest neutrino mass state. The study further reveals that big Bang nucleosynthesis's tightest limits on the neutrino mean square radius cannot exceed $10^{-5}$ times the electron Compton length. Open-source software for computational finance has experienced notable advancements, thanks in part to high-performance computing techniques. This research focuses on enhancing the matrix operations found in the Octave and MATLAB programming environments, specifically on stations equipped with Graphics Processing Units. By leveraging the g08 library, a high-speed linear algebra library developed by the NVIDIA Corporation, this research aims to investigate the performance enhancements derived from introducing parallel computing methods into finite difference methods for option pricing. The results revealed a significant boost in speed, ranging from 15 to 90 times faster, depending on the GPU model used, its operating temperature, and the size of the pricing problem. However, it was also found that the performance gains varied significantly due to several factors, including but not limited to, the model of the GPU, the temperature at which it was operating, and the size of the pricing problem. Consequently, this research offers a range of strategies for optimizing the introduction of parallel algorithms into existing financial risk calculation tools. The most effective approach appears to be completely re-writing the existing code that solves linear algebra problems, rather than relying on legacy code that requires significant modifications to run efficiently on GPU hardware. The techniques explored in this research could also be applied to other programming environments beyond Octave and MATLAB. We investigate how agents can effectively select tasks to complete from a choice of options, by utilizing a decision-making approach that takes into consideration the perceived difficulty of each task. This approach is tested in a scenario where agents have access to the difficulty levels of tasks, but only to a limited extent, mirroring real-world challenges where obtaining comprehensive information about all options can be impractical. Our research focuses on analyzing the performance of agents in a system that is influenced by a task selection process producing random groups of tasks. We examine the outcomes of combining different strategies for selecting tasks of varying difficulty levels and observe how they are affected by the distribution of difficulty levels and the size of the tasks groups. Our findings demonstrate that an approach to evaluating expected value can lead to optimal performance in a static environment but results in poor performance in dynamic environments. In contrast, an alternative approach that considers the worst-case scenario can yield superior results in environments with difficult tasks and small group sizes. However, it becomes less effective in environments with easy tasks and large group sizes. We further contribute an analytical model explaining our observations on how different difficulty level distributions impact the performance of the agents and provide guidelines for selecting the best evaluation approach based on the difficulty level distribution. This research is an exploration of an open problem identified in a previously published paper. The findings presented here are relevant to other domains that involve evaluating expected value in complex multi-agent systems. The approach developed here is applicable to solving problems of interest in the domain of complex systems and could be adapted for use in other domains such as economics and logic-based systems. To tackle high-luminosity collision data, a suite of new precision strategies for theoretical calculations will be implemented. This development will be driven by cutting-edge particle colliders such as CLIC, HL-lhc, ILC, LHeC, LHC, future e+e- colliders, and others. A key aspect of these strategies involves developing techniques to handle multiple unclustered photons in theoretical interpretations of new physics phenomena. To address this challenge, we propose a precision strategy for unresolved photons that utilizes existing clustering information from the detector. This approach, underpinned by the Soft Collinear Approximation, introduces new theoretical tools to address multiple soft photons. We apply this strategy to a range of high-luminosity scenarios and show that it can significantly enhance the sensitivity of searches for new physics phenomena. This strategy also has the added benefit of seamlessly integrating with existing approaches to handle multiple clustered photons. As such, it is fully compatible with the vast majority of existing new physics interpretations that rely on the (modified) 4-momentum approach. Consequently, this precision strategy for unresolved photons is poised to play a major role in the theoretical interpretation of high-luminosity collision data. This is particularly significant, given that a substantial proportion of future new physics discoveries will involve long-lived particles that ultimately decay into one or more photons. This leads to the possibility of resolving neutral new physics states that comprise multiple particles decaying into two or more unresolved photons. In such scenarios, the proposed precision strategy for unresolved photons is expected to play a key role in extracting key properties of these particles, including their mass, decay length, and branching ratios. As an illustration of this capability, we present several scenarios involving long-lived neutral top quarks or vector bosons that can be probed by CLIC or the HL-lhc, relying heavily on the ability to handle multiple unresolved photons. This development is anticipated to have far-reaching implications for the theoretical interpretation of future high-luminosity collision data. As such, this precision strategy is being made publicly available as an open-source code package called 'TheWire'. This code package is fully compatible with the popular MadGraph5_aMC@NLO event generator and is poised to significantly enhance the sensitivity of searches for new physics phenomena involving long-lived particles that decay into one or more photons. As a result, 'TheWire' is expected to play a major role in the theoretical interpretation of future high-luminosity collision data. Approximate kernel methods like Random Fourier Features (RFF) and Pseudo-Random Fourier Features (PRFF) have gained popularity for their ease of use and efficient feature dimension reduction. While PRFF's (pseudo-random) technique for minimizing approximation error has been shown to outperform traditional RFF in terms of both feature dimension reduction and predictive performance, PRFF's name doesn't accurately reflect its methodology. In this paper, we correct the terminology by referring to these methods as Approximate Kernel Embeddings (AKEs), use the term PRFF to represent the specific algorithm that this paper has enhanced, and introduce the term Uniform AKE (UAKE) to describe a newly derived algorithm that also minimizes the approximation error. Unlike previous AKEs, UAKE does not rely on matrix inversion or the Cholesky decomposition, making it suitable for large-scale datasets. In experiments, UAKE outperforms both traditional RFF and PRFF in terms of predictive performance, or matches PRFF's performance at a significantly reduced dimensionality. This work has been accepted as a oral presentation at ICML 2022.

The concept of Cartesian Decomposition (CD) has been previously characterized for complex flag manifolds under the action of reductive groups, and we extend this to the case of real and complex partial flag manifolds. We demonstrate that a partial flag manifold admits a Cartesian Decomposition if and only if it possesses a regular action from a reductive group or if it is a product of spaces affected by a diagonal group action, where these spaces have been subjected to CD transformations. Consequently, we derive the geometric criteria for CD in the real and complex cases. Furthermore, we establish the equivalence between CD and the 'Cartesian Product Structure' (CPS) on partial flag manifolds. Lastly, we determine the CPS structure for a variety of partial flag manifolds. 

In the process, we establish the relationship between the Schubert calculus and the study of CD and CPS structures. We utilize this connection to solve several Schubert calculus problems, including computing the top Schubert class of a 2-step partial flag manifold of type A and determining the Schubert calculus ring of a 3-step partial flag manifold of type A, where the coefficients reveal a connection to Catalan numbers. 

The research described here is the outcome of an extended period of collaboration with the second author, who regrettably passed away during the writing stage. His intellectual contributions played a significant role in the research outlined here. The remaining authors are grateful for the valuable insights he provided and acknowledge his influence on the work. 

The paper is divided into two main parts. Section 1 introduces key concepts, including partial flag manifolds, Schubert varieties, and the Grassmannian matrix Gamma, while also exploring the properties of Cartesian Decomposition and its relationship to the action of reductive groups and diagonal groups. In this section, we also determine the CD structures for various partial flag manifolds and establish the connection between CD, CPS, and Schubert calculus. 

In Part II, we delve deeper into specific examples, including 1-Ackermann subvarieties, Schubert cycles in G/G_t, Schubert cycles in Sp_{2n}/Sp_{2n-2}, and Schubert cycles in SO_{2n}/SO_{2n-2). We also compute the top Schubert class of a 2-step partial flag manifold of type A and examine the Schubert calculus ring of a 3-step partial flag manifold of type A. The coefficients in this ring reveal a connection to Catalan numbers

Human language understanding is inherently complex due to varying contexts and numerous word forms, which is further compounded by limited data availability in many languages. This complexity presents significant obstacles for machines learning to comprehend language. In an effort to investigate potential solutions to this issue, we examined the challenges of modeling context and word forms within a language using both theoretical and practical approaches. By drawing on existing literature and conducting additional research, we sought to answer two primary questions: first, how do context and word forms influence each other in a language; and second, what strategies can be employed to effectively model their interactions. Through an exploration of both shallow and deep language aspects, we assessed the impact of context and word forms on meaning and tested various models that combine contextual and formal representations to capture their interactions. Our results showed that models incorporating both contextual and formal information can better grasp the intricate relationships between words and their contexts than models focusing solely on context or formal aspects. This finding suggests that future research should prioritize developing models that effectively combine multiple information sources to effectively model the intricate interactions within languages and learn from limited datasets. This work is a initial step towards addressing the fundamental challenges posed by the complexity of languages and necessitates a continued exploration of novel approaches in conjunction with the ongoing advancements in machine learning and language representation. In this paper, a new nonorthogonal uplink protocol, called NOVR-XL, is proposed to enhance random access in large-scale millimeter wave systems. NOVR-XL takes advantage of the properties of XL-MIMO systems and introduces a new technique for generating unique sequences, leading to a significant reduction in sequence-generated signal transmission. Simulations demonstrate that the NOVR-XL protocol results in a substantial increase in random access throughput and moderate increases in detection complexity and interference resilience, outperforming a previously proposed protocol, NOVR. System performance with NOVR-XL can be further optimized by applying different receive antenna combinations, particularly those with low combiner complexity. Simulation results confirm that NOVR-XL achieves a notable increase in random access performance under moderate to high traffic conditions, ultimately requiring only moderate increases in detection complexity and interference resilience. The performance of NOVR-XL can be enhanced by incorporating new sequence-generated signal detection methods, known as metasurface-aided techniques, which offer enhanced detection performance without significant increases in complexity. Ultimately, the NOVR-XL protocol is shown to achieve a significant increase in random access performance in XL-MIMO systems.

Investigating correlated electrons in transition metal oxides like strontium manganese oxide, SrMnO$_3$, is crucial due to the diverse effects resulting from correlated electrons in these materials. To tackle this problem, we employ the full canonical transformation method to develop an effective single-particle model that accounts for both on-site interactions and delocalized orbital correlations. This model exhibits a spectral structure characterized by multiple bands, and we demonstrate its connection to the lattice model using the sum rule of the spectral weight. Numerical calculations of this model yield results similar to those obtained from Gutzwiller theory, particularly regarding the one-electron levels and density of states. Additionally, our model correctly reproduces the lattice model's crystal field splitting and orbital correlation-induced shifts. To further understand its implications, we explore the effective one-body potential derived from this model and analyze its relation to the lattice model's density of states and Fermi surface. This effective potential reveals an intricate band structure influenced by both the crystal field and orbital correlations, resulting in shifts that differ significantly from those predicted by the Gutzwiller approach. This difference arises due to the distinct ways these models treat orbital correlations, with potential implications for the physics of SrMnO$_3$, such as charge/orbital order and superconductivity in other correlated materials. Overall, our study provides an effective single-particle description of the electron structure of SrMnO$_3$ that can be utilized to analyze and understand other transition metal oxides with similar physics. This new perspective on correlated electrons offers opportunities to revisit existing theories of these materials. As an illustration, we discuss the potential applications of this model to order formation in SrMnO$_3$. This analysis emphasizes the importance of molecular sensitivity in Molmer-Sorensen gates and suggests a method for creating robust gates for polyatomic molecules. By examining a model molecule based on $^{88}$Sr$_2$, we demonstrate how a faulty high-resolution gate can be converted into an effective tool for creating entanglement in a molecular system. Specifically, in a chain of two-electron beams, we observed a significant increase in entanglement development when using a frequency-insensitive gate design, thanks to the overlapping of faulty gate components. This finding suggests the possibility of successful entanglement accumulation through deliberate design of frequency-robust Molmer-Sorensen gates, paving the way for efficient quantum computations with complex molecules. Furthermore, our research indicates that such frequency robustness can be achieved with minimal loss of efficiency, involving only a minor increase in beam frequencies and powers. Ultimately, this study provides a crucial framework for adapting Molmer-Sorensen gates to various types of polyatomic molecules.  This research is relevant to the field as it offers an essential solution to one of the primary obstacles in quantum computations with molecules. The work builds upon an earlier finding showing that ion chains experience uncontrolled shifts in energy levels due to laser coupling, effectively limiting the reliability of Molmer-Sorensen gates. In response to this issue, our research offers a groundbreaking solution by describing the explicit implementation of frequency-robust Molmer-Sorensen gates. Reconstructing a 3D face from multiple 2D faces of a single individual is a challenging task.  Faces can have significant variations in their inherent geometry, which remains unchanged despite changes in facial expression and pose.  Recent studies have made notable progress on this topic by learning 3D faces and factor analysis but are typically limited to faces of European descent and often rely on extensive training datasets.  Our proposed framework, Self-aligned Dual Face Regression Network (SADRNet), models 3D faces as a combination of pose-dependent and pose-independent factors while eliminating the need for training datasets.  SADRNet takes a single 2D face as input and estimates two factors: the pose-independent factor, representing the inherent geometry of the face, and the pose-dependent factor, which combines the face's rotational orientation and morphological changes.  Our network architecture includes an alignment module, where a rotation-agnostic coordinate system is established to facilitate the disentanglement of pose-dependent and pose-independent factors.  A nested context aggregation module is introduced to learn an end-to-end 3D face representation from a 2D face.  Experimental evaluations of our framework demonstrate superior performance on various datasets, surpassing state-of-the-art methods that rely on supervised training.  Our work provides an unprecedented level of disentanglement of pose-dependent and pose-independent factors, achieved without relying on extensive training datasets or annotated rotation information.  Our method's ability to operate in real-time makes it suitable for numerous real-world applications, such as video compression, facial animation, and virtual try-on.  Our framework's code and dataset are available online at https://github.com/cglierh/SADRNet.  Our work has been featured in CVPR 2020 Workshop on Advances in Multi-camera Facial Behavior Analysis and was awarded the Best Demo Award at the CVPR 2020 Workshop on Facial Behavior in Social Contexts.  Our demo can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6cY6s5kQx9A.  Our work has been covered by various media outlets, including Science Daily, TechNode, and CNBeta. High-dimensional linear models can yield substantial insights when dealing with complex, infinite-dimensional data. However, typical applications face significant challenges when observing time-dependent variables or having infinite data dimensions. To overcome these challenges, we present novel estimators and theoretical findings that enable us to directly work with time-dependent variables and use the entire data set, rather than relying on random sampling. Specifically, we demonstrate that our estimators can effectively recover the infinite-dimensional parameters and the model parameters by applying a unique low-rank constraint and an alternating minimization technique. Our theoretical results provide a fixed-time convergence guarantee and a rate of convergence that depends on the rank constraint, achieving the optimal rate of $\sqrt{T}$, where T represents the total number of observations. Through simulated scenarios and a real-world experiment, we showcase the superior performance of our time-dependent estimators, demonstrating significant improvements over current methods. Additionally, our results highlight the advantages of using the entire data set for estimations, leading to average prediction errors that are nearly 50% lower than those obtained from randomly selected data sets. Moreover, our approach offers enhanced robustness in model parameter recoveries. In conclusion, our novel estimators and algorithms offer compelling benefits, yielding superior performance and outperforming existing methods across various scenarios. Moreover, our method's ability to handle the most general linear models makes it an appealing solution. Current active learning methodologies often rely on random sampling or slight modifications thereof. However, these methods fail to account for the significant scale differences between large datasets like ImageNet and the smaller benchmark datasets they're typically tested on. As a result, traditional approaches can select unrepresentative, easily classifiable images for labeling, thus misrepresenting the performance of newer classification methods. This study introduces PoolRank, an active learning framework based on a score-driven approach that prioritizes the selection of challenging images. PoolRank utilizes a scoring model that assesses images based on their predicted class probability and selects those requiring most significant decision-making by the classifier. Experimental results demonstrate that PoolRank significantly outperforms existing active learning methods on ImageNet when evaluating the representative difficulty of selected images. Moreover, PoolRank is particularly effective in exploiting diverse, challenging images to achieve high performance, as evident from our mixed model evaluations. Furthermore, PoolRank shows its versatility by being applicable to various baseline models and extending to active learning tasks beyond classification. The source code for this project is available online at https://github.com/ziangco/PoolRank.

This paper presents an innovative algorithm for power allocation and scheduling in highly dynamic Time Division Duplex (TDD) systems, targeted at maximizing uplink throughput in cellular networks. The method is designed to address the complex challenges posed by rapidly changing TDD configurations, cell load variations, and distant TDD cycles. To overcome these difficulties, the algorithm leverages an optimized coexistence strategy, cooperative scheduling, and dynamic power allocation. Through mathematical proof, the proposed method guarantees maximum uplink throughput in highly dynamic TDD systems and effectively addresses interference between neighboring cells. To improve computational efficiency, the algorithm includes a fast iteration mechanism to converge quickly. Empirical studies confirm the method's effectiveness, showcasing a substantial increase in uplink throughput and reduced computational complexity. The algorithm outperforms existing approaches, such as dynamic TDD, interference alignment, and cooperative schemes, and is applicable to various TDD cycle configurations. The algorithm's convergence speed is optimized for small to medium-sized networks, achieving optimal performance after just a few iterations. The proposed method exhibits superior performance in terms of computational complexity, outperforming other algorithms by several orders of magnitude, and is therefore well-suited for large-scale cellular networks. The method's feasibility is demonstrated through simulation on a small to medium-sized network, and the code is available online for further evaluation. The research is relevant to current and future cellular networks, including 5G and 6G, characterized by dynamic and multi-band TDD configurations. The method is highly adaptable and compatible with various network architectures, radio access technologies, and future multi-band TDD configurations. We examined the effects of an external magnetic field on the behavior of normalized cumulants of the Ising model on a Cayley tree using a genetic algorithm to optimize parameters. Our study focused on the spin glass phase and the equilibrium system at positive external magnetic field values. We found that applying a small positive external magnetic field causes the critical temperature to decrease. As the field strength increases, the critical temperature remains relatively stable before eventually decreasing. We observed similar patterns in normalized cumulant behavior and susceptibility for both the spin glass and equilibrium systems. In equilibrium, higher field strengths lead to increased shifts in the critical temperature and susceptibility, while the spin glass phase exhibits a more stable critical temperature and susceptibility before they begin to increase at higher field strengths. These changes occur without altering the shape of the normalized cumulant curves. Our findings also demonstrate that the Ising model on a Cayley tree exhibits first-order phase transition when the external magnetic field exceeds a certain threshold. This threshold corresponds to the field at which the critical temperature begins to increase in negative values. We calculated this threshold value to be approximately 0.73 in magnetic unit for the spin glass phase. Our study provides magnetic field protocols that can be applied to similar studies using optimization techniques. Moreover, our research offers theoretical expressions for normalized cumulants, susceptibility, and the derivative of the free energy in the equilibrium system for positive external magnetic field values. These expressions can be particularly useful for understanding the behavior of the cumulants in the equilibrium system. Our study also compares the effects of an external magnetic field on the Ising model to those of a heat bath bias, which exhibits a more stable critical temperature with increased bias strength. Finally, we discussed the limitations of our research and potential avenues for further investigation. These investigations could explore other optimization algorithms or examine the behavior of the cumulants in the canonical ensemble. Additionally, our study could be extended to more complex lattice structures or to models beyond the Ising model. These extensions hold significant potential for revealing the underlying behaviors driving our findings. Our study provides a theoretical framework that can be applied to a broader range of systems exhibiting phase transitions. Moreover, many of our theoretical expressions hold value in understanding the behavior of the cumulants in the equilibrium system, even in the absence of an external magnetic field. Lastly, our study highlights the effectiveness of genetic algorithms in optimizing parameters for systems undergoing phase transitions, a technique with implications for other research scenarios. These scenarios include multi-objective optimization problems involving transition temperature and an additional parameter affecting the behavior of the cumulants.

We examine a specific class of 4-tensors that maintain their invariance under certain types of unitary transformations known as topological twists, and demonstrate their fundamental role in describing matrix product operators within 2-dimensional systems that exhibit topological properties. Utilizing a combination of inductive methods and detailed analysis of their structure, we establish an exhaustive categorization of all relevant 4-tensors by identifying their distinct forms and determining the underlying algebraic structures that govern their behavior. Furthermore, we develop a procedure for computing the eigenvalues and corresponding eigenstates for a given set of matrix product operators, and demonstrate the applicability of our findings through numerical simulations of a specific lattice system. Our research provides a comprehensive framework for exploring matrix product operators within systems that exhibit topological properties, enabling the systematic investigation of symmetry-protected boundary phases and the diagnosis of topological order in 2-dimensional lattices. This framework can be employed for the analytical study of systems lacking topological twists, and we discuss various methods for extending our theory to account for multiple topological twists and interacting electrons within lattice systems. Furthermore, we discuss potential applications of our theory to systems of linked particles and lattice systems featuring non-trivial topological twists. Additionally, we outline the connections between our 4-tensor framework and other theoretical formalisms, including the fusion category theory, and propose the extension of our framework to account for both intrinsic and extrinsic symmetries within matrix product operators. This proposed extension is demonstrated through the analysis of a specific lattice system featuring both intrinsic and extrinsic symmetries. Lastly, we outline the relationships between the eigenvalues of matrix product operators and the topological invariants of corresponding toric boundary phases, and discuss the implications of our findings for the diagnosis of topological order in systems that exhibit significant spin-orbit coupling. Airports have a high demand for advanced techniques to identify prohibited items quickly, accurately, and with minimal false alarms. Although deep learning-based methods have achieved significant success in image processing, there is a lack of suitable datasets for training models on the detection of prohibited items. To address this issue, we created HiXray, a comprehensive dataset consisting of X-ray images of 19 prohibited items, including explosives, firearms, knives, and scissors. HiXray contains a unique combination of real-world images that mimic the diversity of items found in actual luggage, along with associated bounding boxes and class labels. We evaluated the effectiveness of hi, a state-of-the-art deep learning model designed for boundary detection, on this dataset and found it to yield impressive results. When fine-tuned on the training data, hi achieved a precision rate of 51.43%, a recall rate of 61.53%, and a mean aperture (MAP) score of 45.91%. Moreover, our experiments demonstrated the benefits of adapting the model to account for x-ray distortions and variations, ultimately resulting in improved performance. HiXray is an essential contribution to the community working on x-ray-based detection systems and is openly accessible for researchers to develop and evaluate their approaches. Furthermore, we released a prototype of an automated scoring system called ScoreX, in conjunction with the dataset, to provide comprehensive evaluation and facilitate fair comparison among methods. This system is designed to be flexible and adaptable to different datasets and algorithms. We also highlighted significant achievements achieved by leading research teams utilizing HiXray, including the top-performing model, ScoreX, and a cutting-edge approach incorporating edge detection and segmentation. Ultimately, our work aims to accelerate the adoption of advanced detection technologies in airport security by providing HiXray and promoting an open discussion on challenging real-world problems. The dataset, accompanying benchmark results, and the prototype scoring system are available at https://hixray.org.

When dealing with sensitive data represented as graph structures, learning a model from this data while ensuring privacy protection proves complicated due to unknown connections between data points. This complication arises because traditional differential privacy methods rely on nearby relationships between data points to set appropriate hyperparameters, which is not a factor in graph structures. In our research, we address this issue by developing a method to compute privacy loss in comparison to the closest neighbors in a graph, which can be used to establish a private margin for linear models and therefore prevent overfitting. Our approach involves utilizing the shortest path length as a measure of proximity between data points and modifying the definition of neighboring sets based on this distance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to private linear regression and feature learning on various types of graph structures. The results show our method to compute privacy loss outperforms existing techniques in terms of accuracy and model performance. Furthermore, our approach enables private model evaluation through feedback from data owners, which can be reached without requiring significant modifications to existing deep learning frameworks. Our source code is available for review at our GitHub repository.

Music recommendation systems typically rely on user data and song correlations, which are often derived from explicit user feedback, such as ratings and history logs. This paper explores the use of audio content analysis to create personalized playlists for individual listeners. It discusses the development of an end-to-end system that leverages audio content analysis to extract semantic features from music tracks and applies these features to cluster users and create playlists. The system consists of multiple modules, including audio feature extraction, dimension reduction, bi-temporal similarity learning, user clustering, and playlist creation. This approach enables the generation of personalized playlists without requiring explicit user data or song correlations. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this system in creating distinctive playlists for individual listeners. Furthermore, the system is adaptable to various music genres and can operate on a large dataset of over 10,000 tracks. The technology behind this system has been deployed in a real-world application, showcasing its capability to create personalized playlists that are publicly accessible. In addition, the system's audio features and user clustering methodology are also applicable to other areas, such as sound event classification and cross-domain clustering. This work offers a comprehensive solution for creating personalized playlists through audio content analysis and can serve as a foundation for further research and development in music information retrieval. This approach has the potential to revolutionize music recommendation systems by producing high-quality playlists without requiring explicit user data or song correlations. This could significantly simplify the process of creating personalized music playlists for music streaming platforms and voice assistants, making music more accessible and enjoyable for individual listeners. This technology can be particularly useful for users who are new to a music streaming platform or have limited listening history. In such cases, audio content analysis-based playlists can provide a more personalized starting point for their music discovery journey. In addition, this approach can be used to create playlists for specific events, such as holiday playlists or playlists for particular moods. This is achieved by applying the system to specific audio tracks that embody the desired characteristics and clustering users who share similar semantic features with these tracks. In an experimental setting, this approach produced playlists with high quality and uniqueness. Unobstructed movement in an environment inhabited by other agents requires robots to avoid collisions with those agents. A prominent approach in collision detection and obstacle avoidance utilizes repulsive forces, originating from potential fields created by considering the distance between agents. However, traditional field methods are only effective within a predefined range and can result in infinite forces when reached. To address these limitations, a new framework based on vortex fields is proposed. This approach redefines the repulsive potential field to increase with area instead of distance, resulting in controlled forces that act over a broader range. A mathematical analysis of vortex fields shows that they conform to the proposed robot interaction model, and this model's properties ensure that robot movements maintain continuity. To demonstrate the feasibility of this approach, a sample implementation using Unreal Engine 4 and the PhysX physics engine is provided. Comparative testing with existing methods indicates that vortex fields result in successful collisions avoidance using a significantly reduced adjustment factor. The proposed framework offers a foundation for developing more sophisticated collision avoidance systems, and its modifiable nature allows it to be adapted for various multi-agent applications. Deep neural networks are designed to ignore irrelevant classes, but this ability is compromised when they encounter novel classes. The problem of learning new classes without affecting previous performance is a well-known challenge in continual learning and the open-world paradigm. 

The study presented here examines a fundamental approach to continual learning: the Nearest Mean Classifier. This method continuously learns new classes by updating their mean values and recalibrating the decision boundary in a data-driven manner. The evaluation is conducted across multiple datasets, assessing the performance of the Nearest Mean Classifier against state-of-the-art continual learning methods that leverage external memory. Notably, the experiments demonstrate that the Nearest Mean Classifier can achieve comparable or better results when using pre-trained models from the Transformer family. The study also explores various expansion scenarios and finds that the method's performance holds significant potential for the open-world learning scenario. The code and data used in the experiments are available under an open-source license.

Deep neural networks are widely applied in various aspects of life but the complexity of their training processes poses a significant challenge. To overcome this issue, a sub-class of neural networks known as Teacher-Student (T-S) architectures has gained popularity as it facilitates the training of lightweight student networks that can achieve high performance. During training, a more complex teacher network with high accuracy is trained while a less complex student network is trained to mimic the teacher by reducing the cross-entropy loss and minimizing the difference in their predictions. The goal is to ensure the student network can achieve high performance similar to the teacher network. The main issue with existing T-S architectures is the high computational cost of training both the teacher and student networks. To address this challenge, we propose a novel T-S architecture known as the Iterative Teacher-Student (ITS) network that trains the teacher and student networks sequentially rather than in parallel. The proposed ITS network system consists of multiple training loops called super-training loops where each super-training loop comprises the training of a teacher network followed by the training of multiple student networks. The key aspect of the proposed ITS network is the introduction of an iterative distortion regularization (IDR) loss that allows the student and teacher networks to have different classes and can be applied to any given T-S architecture. The experimental results show that the proposed ITS network achieves higher performance and lower computational cost compared to state-of-the-art T-S architectures such as Knowledge Distillation (KD) and Dual Teacher-Student (DT-S) networks. The proposed ITS network system is also demonstrated to be applicable to various deep neural network architectures including convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural networks. The code of the proposed ITS network is publicly available online.

The complex velocity distribution of Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs) as they approach Earth during seasonal WIMP flux variations is analyzed in depth. In our study, we examine the relationship between the WIMP velocity field and their interaction with Earth during their approach. We observe that Earth's gravitational interaction with WIMPs has a significant effect on their velocity distribution as they approach. As a result, WIMPs that interact with Earth have a higher average velocity when they are at their closest point to Earth. This is because these WIMPs have a higher velocity when they begin their approach and as a result, experience a stronger gravitational pull from Earth, causing them to have a closer approach distance. This effect is particularly pronounced for a specific one-dimensional velocity distribution of WIMPs, often referred to as the 'cadmium profile', which implies an irregular seasonal variation in WIMP-induced low energy neutrino events. In contrast, this effect is relatively minimal for the overall velocity distribution of incident halo WIMPs and thus, does not significantly impact the commonly accepted'velocities of flight' model which explains observed high velocity WIMP interactions with Earth. In addition, our study reveals that deep underground WIMP detection facilities such as LUX can utilize a novel complementary approach to optimize their sensitivity to WIMP-induced low energy neutrino interactions with light nuclei such as helium or carbon. This approach involves analyzing seasonal variations in the detected event rate at these facilities. In such analyses, significant Compton scattering events within the scintillator detector material can be accounted for with a reliable simulation method. As a result, this approach can provide these facilities with an additional research perspective that is entirely independent of their primary direct detection research methods. In the context of the LUX1.4 data set, our study reveals that there may exist a slight deviation from the expected velocity distribution of incident halo WIMPs and as a result, there may exist a small seasonal variation in the detected event rate at these facilities. Consequently, utilizing larger data sets from future deep underground WIMP detection facilities such as LUX-DarkSide or WOLF-DR will be necessary in order to verify or contradict this study's findings. A key limitation of traditional linear sampling methods, like the PSLS, lies in their reliance on straight-line connections, which fails to account for curved light paths, particularly in imaging systems utilizing thick entrance windows. This research introduces rCASPR, a refined sampling approach that utilizes reference curves to accurately model radiation transport, even in the presence of complex light distributions. Unlike traditional methods, rCASPR does not restrict sampled points to linear paths, enabling a more precise representation of light dispersion. Evaluations indicate that rCASPR yields a more precise point-spread function and contrast replica, directly benefiting Monte Carlo-sourced images. Furthermore, rCASPR demonstrates its ability to handle various types of reference curves, such as tangents, facilitating a more accurate assessment of sampling efficiency. Monte Carlo simulations verify that rCASPR's performance can be up to four times more efficient than the linear sampling method, depending on the imaging system and object size. Lastly, rCASPR is evaluated on real-world data, demonstrating its capacity to generate accurate contrast replicas and improve Monte Carlo-image contrast via projected angle sampling and projection-based data rejection. The proposed approach also offers a potential solution to accelerate iterative algorithms for system inversion. The rCASPR algorithm is openly accessible online.

This study examines the recent shift from shipping cartels to independent freighters in the Middle East, specifically focusing on the implications for freighter sales prices and operating rates. Adaptive approximation techniques, such as sparse approximation and compressive sensing, have been successfully applied to reduce high-dimensional signals, overcoming previous barriers. However, the performance of these methods can deteriorate when the sampling process adapts to the signal's structure and together they defy traditional estimation methods. In contrast, our research introduces a novel adaptive technique known as Annihilated Compressive Random Sampling (ACRS), which achieves precise reconstruction of reduced-dimensional signals even when the sampling process is fully aligned with the signal. Unlike traditional methods, ACRS's performance does not decline in the presence of adaptive sampling. Additionally, our research establishes the theoretical foundations required for ACRS's construction and proves its effectiveness through computational validation. The results show that ACRS's performance can be optimized by controlling the parameters that define it and that it can effectively handle various signal structures and sampling scenarios. For instance, ACRS can accurately reconstruct signals composed of Dirac Comb functions, wrapped Gaussian processes, and fractional Brownian motion. Moreover, ACRS's performance can be enhanced by incorporating prior knowledge about the signal's structure. In conclusion, our research presents ACRS as a robust and adaptable dimensionality reduction technique capable of handling complex high-dimensional signals. ACRS's construction is grounded in non-degenerate matrix theory and is shown to be computationally efficient. The approach has the potential to be applied across a broad spectrum of signal processing scenarios.

We have demonstrated that such associated geometries are comprised of surfaces with the property of being locally conformal to the original domain, and this property is both necessary and sufficient for the associated geometries to be compact and smooth across all points, except for a set measuring zero in dimension. Furthermore, this condition for compactness is both necessary and sufficient in the case of Eulerian tilts without restrictions on curvature. This paper explores a novel approach to an aggregation algorithm that facilitates two-way communication between an aggregator and a discrete set of loads, allowing the sharing of maximum entropy feedback information. We demonstrate that by utilizing this feedback, an aggregator can efficiently optimize the discrete loads to obtain a desired probability distribution, which directly correlates with their total energy output. Furthermore, we showcase that incorporating negative terms into the utility function enables us to replicate any given discrete probability distribution. We evaluate the performance of the algorithm under varying parameters and examine its efficacy in addressing real-world scalability challenges. The results indicate that the algorithm achieves optimal outcomes under conditions of low connectivity, even when faced with an infinite number of loads. We also highlight an interesting connection to the Walrasian auction algorithm and present methods for mitigating over-excitation issues caused by feedback maximization. The findings are supported by numerical data and case studies from modern power grids. Finally, we outline potential directions for further research and extensions to the existing approach.

The appreciation of precise financial forecasts relies heavily on accurate initial conditions, specifically historical prices and trading indicators. Consequently, developing efficient methods for estimating these variables is crucial. This study presents novel formulas for calculating technical indicators on publicly accessible financial platforms, utilizing high-frequency data and interpolating missing price observations. Technical indicators typically exhibit linear relationships with time, allowing for easy extrapolation. An examination of their performance in predicting stock movements across various time frames is also conducted. Findings demonstrate that models based on these new estimations yield greater accuracy than traditional methods, particularly when taking into consideration the biases associated with overstepping. This research provides a framework for enhancing financial modeling, and collectible stocks are among the applicable areas. An illustrative example involving the collection of stocks from the S\&P 500 index is included. An open-source implementation of the proposed methods is available online.

We examine double Higgs production in the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT), focusing on the impact of operators influencing $h\gamma\gamma$ and $hgg$ interactions. This analysis is carried out within the Heavy Resonance Framework (HRF), a power-counting approach for effectively describing higher-order processes in the SMEFT. By comparing the HRF to the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SEFT), we identify the relevant effective theory operators and determine the coefficient relationships between them. We find that leading-order HRF coefficients can be directly linked to their SMEFT counterparts, and this connection allows us to interpret the effects of dimension-five and six operators on double Higgs production. Furthermore, we find that the resonant contribution to this process can be understood through a simple effective theory description, given the mass and couplings of a heavy scalar resonance that decays into a pair of Higgs bosons. We also provide explicit resonance parameterizations for various heavy scalar scenarios, including the $\rho$-parity violating $a_0$ and $f_0$ scenarios, and discuss how these frameworks can be utilized for interpreting double Higgs production in search experiments at future colliders like HL-LLP and CLIC. Finally, we recognize that comprehensive simulations are necessary to accurately assess the detectability of new physics in this channel at these colliders. Still, our study lays the groundwork for developing efficient strategies to achieve this understanding. Our investigation yields an analytical big-bang universe model characterized by a non-singular beginning that transitions to a non-relativistic phase. The 'pre-non-relativistic' phase is distinguished, allowing for an analytical expansion in powers of $H_{\min}t$ within the framework of Einstein gravity. This approach bypasses utilizing a series of approximate solutions. The newly defined parameters $a(t)$, $p(t)$, and $q(t)$ are identified, revealing that during the 'pre-non-relativistic' era, the universe exhibits an almost constant $K$ behavior, with $a(t)$ expanding in a manner akin to $H_{\min}t$. The transition to the non-relativistic phase is analyzed in detail. The newly introduced parameters $p(t)$ and $q(t)$ take on values that mirror the characteristics of the Einstein-de Sitter and matter-dominated phases. The investigation of the Einstein-Boltzmann equations yields an expression for the Hubble parameter $H_{\min}$ in terms of the present-day cosmological parameters. The findings lead to the derivation of an equation of state $p(t)$ that bridges the non-singular big-bang universe to the present day. The proposed model may provide a framework for reinterpreting the phenomena observed in the early universe. Moreover, it paves the way for investigating initial conditions of the universe prior to big-bang singularities. The model may also be expanded to account for additional fundamental forces such as quantum gravity. The extensions to the present study will be the subject of forthcoming investigations. The proposed approach to the early universe can be contrasted with the 'brake' approach, the 'early dark energy' scenario, and the related cosmological parameters adjustments as evaluated in the existing literature. The implications of the new model for gravitational waves and the primordial power spectrum of cosmological perturbations will be the focus of subsequent analyses. The model is compatible with present observational constraints. It is notable that the investigations of the Einstein-Boltzmann equations led to the derivation of an expression for $H_{\min}$, implying that $H_{\min}$ is not an arbitrarily chosen parameter. Rather, it is possible to obtain $H_{\min} \approx 0.27$ nm/s/Upc, significantly below the estimated value for the Hubble constant $H_0 \approx 0.67$ Upc. The model introduces the concept of 'ental relativity', which is distinct from conventional entropy-based relativity.

Using high-resolution near-infrared spectroscopy from VLT/MADRID and VLT/KI, we've studied the ionized gas outflows in two starburst galaxies from the legacy survey LEGACYS. These galaxies exhibit large gas reserves and moderate to high star formation rates. Observations show that both galaxies have gas flowing at high velocities from their centers, likely caused by supernova explosions and stellar mergers. One galaxy, LEGACYS-01, has a significant outflow channel, revealing an outflow map in the H-beta and H-I lines, which indicates a rotating disk and possible wind effects. Another galaxy, LEGACYS-02, shows an outflow map in the [FeII] lines, which indicates a wind with a different velocity and possible interactions between gas streams. By analyzing outflow maps, we found that both galaxies have outflows that hinder gas turnover, resulting in gas reserves being converted into stars within 100 million years. This process is enhanced by massive star bursts, which turn gas into stars over 10-20 years. As a result, both galaxies are generating massive stellar reserves, which are the result of their intense star bursts that are transforming their gas reserves into stellar reserves. These observations highlight the influence of ionized gas outflows on galaxy evolution, which is driven by massive star bursts that turn gas into stars, which are the basis of universal stellar mass growth. Upcoming high-resolution spectrographs will allow us to monitor the effects of massive star bursts and galaxy mergers on galaxy evolution. This will provide us with a deeper understanding of the mechanisms driving universal stellar mass growth and the chemical evolution of galaxies. Configurations within discrete optimization problems are often evaluated based on their efficiency, which is typically determined by a computationally expensive function. This difficulty is compounded by the vast number of possible configurations, making it impractical to test each individually. To address this challenge, we propose a technique called BoAnon for approximating efficient configurations by leveraging a distinct distribution of configurations, specifically one that is biased towards the most efficient options. This method is distinct from traditional approaches that prioritize exploring novel configurations over retaining existing information. The BoAnon system consists of multiple modules, including one that evaluates the efficacy of drawing configuration sub-components. We demonstrate that our system's evaluation strategy yields configurations that are at least 20 times more efficient than random trials. Furthermore, BoAnon can be applied to any configuration domain that can be represented as a graph, making it a versatile tool for discovering efficient configurations. With this approach, we are able to find configurations that exhibit substantially better performance compared to traditional methods, which becomes especially notable as the size of the search space increases. Additionally, BoAnon can be employed in conjunction with other configuration discovery methods, such as evolutionary algorithms, to create more effective hybrid techniques. We showcase the effectiveness of BoAnon by applying it to the problem of configuring network virtualization, which involves determining the most efficient placement of virtual networks within a physical infrastructure. Our results indicate that BoAnon yields significantly better performance compared to traditional methods and other state-of-the-art configuration solvers. Moreover, BoAnon can evaluate large-scale configurations that cannot be analyzed by traditional methods. Finally, we highlight the fundamental concepts underlying BoAnon and argue that its core ideas are highly relevant to other configuration domains beyond network virtualization. We also provide concrete directions for enhancing BoAnon's performance in specific scenarios. We have made our BoAnon system publicly accessible to facilitate further research and to provide a versatile configuration solver that can be used to tackle a wide range of efficient configuration challenges. We have also made available the source code and experimental data corresponding to our evaluation results. We invite researchers to leverage BoAnon as a basis for developing other efficient configuration solvers and to explore new configuration domains where its principles can be applied. We plan to build upon BoAnon by enhancing its evaluation strategy and exploring new configuration solvers that can be used in conjunction with its components. We also intend to extend BoAnon's applicability to configuration domains that cannot be represented as graph structures. Large-scale RDF datasets pose challenges for quality assessment due to extensive data sizes and nuanced quality standards. Many existing quality evaluation techniques are designed to analyze small to medium-sized datasets and prioritize precision over performance. To overcome these limitations, we present a high-speed, distributed quality evaluation framework called DistQualityAssessment. This framework utilizes a novel approach to evaluate complex quality standards and incorporates a large-scale RDF dataset called EventCloud. Our experiments demonstrate that DistQualityAssessment achieves exceptional performance, evaluating over 8 billion triples in under 100 seconds on a cluster of five machines. Furthermore, our approach demonstrates comparable precision to state-of-the-art quality evaluation techniques like HiBEnQuality and QuadQualityAssessment on medium-sized datasets. However, DistQualityAssessment falls short of these methods in terms of memory consumption, with a peak usage of 6 GB compared to 10 and 24 GB for HiBEnQuality and QuadQualityAssessment, respectively. Nonetheless, DistQualityAssessment offers a high-performance solution for large-scale RDF quality assessment, particularly suitable for evaluating complex standards on massive datasets. The framework and associated data are freely accessible for download. The source code can be found at https://github.com/hpc4gsa/DistQualityAssessment, along with extensive documentation at https://distqualityassessment.hpc.gsa.io/. The EventCloud dataset used in this experiment is available at https://eventcloud.gsa.io/. The framework's evaluation protocols and results are outlined in the accompanying paper, which has been thoroughly reviewed and is now featured in the Journal of Web Semantics under the title "DistQualityAssessment: A High-Performance, Distributed Quality Evaluation Framework for Large-Scale RDF Datasets". The paper can be found at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.websem.2022.100453.

This study explores the properties of minimum density power divergence (MDPD) estimators in relation to maximum likelihood (ML) estimators for independent increment and Markov processes. We examine the behavior of MDPD estimators as the power parameter increases, finding they converge to ML estimators, which require inverting an intense expression. In contrast, MDPD estimators can be calculated directly for many processes, including fractional Brownian motion, Brownian motion with a drift, and alpha-stable processes. Empirical results suggest that MDPD estimators yield similar accuracy to ML estimators when the power parameter is set appropriately, and also demonstrate the advantages of MDPD estimators in modeling multiple independent increment processes with varying dimensions. Furthermore, MDPD is shown to offer greater robustness than ML in modeling certain processes with rare outliers. The benefits of MDPD are attributed to its ability to downweight excessive density data while remaining relatively unbiased. The methodology developed here is applicable to a broad category of models known as independent increment processes, which encompasses a range of processes including alpha-stable processes and their combinations. The methodology is demonstrated through the analysis of a dataset containing various types of financial returns. The findings suggest that MDPD is an appealing estimation method due to its high computational efficiency and the ability to handle complex, multi-dimensional data with ease. The methodology developed here is particularly useful for any analytical methods that rely on density estimators, including kernel-based methods and MDPD itself. We explore how high-energy processes affecting the gas around active galaxies affect their observable characteristics, specifically their optical spectrum, through a computational framework that combines radiative shocks and photoionization. This method allows us to analyze the impact of shock-ionization and its interactions with the surrounding gas, particularly when a radiative shock interacts with a photoionized gas cloud. Our analysis reveals how this process modifies standard ionization patterns, creating distinct patterns of ionized gas regions and altering the observed spectral characteristics, including line strengths and broadening due to turbulence. These effects could provide valuable insights into active galaxies, particularly how they influence their host galaxies. Furthermore, our approach highlights potential variations in active galaxies that arise from the interplay between radiative shocks and photoionization, offering new avenues for observational and theoretical research. By integrating our framework with cosmological simulations, we aim to investigate how radiative shocks influence active galaxies across different mass scales and environmental settings. Nonetheless, our analysis faces significant computational challenges that require the development of optimized algorithms for treating shock-ionization processes within an active galaxy context. By leveraging existing multigrid methods and other techniques, we anticipate significant performance improvements that will enable in-depth studies of active galaxies through gas dynamics simulations. Nonetheless, preliminary findings from our pilot study indicate considerable potential for this approach to shed light on the interplay between radiative shocks, active galaxies, and their surroundings. As such, we outline the architectural enhancements necessary to achieve a major performance boost in future applications. Ultimately, we propose that incorporating active galaxies within the realm of shock-ionization could be addressed by developing customized algorithms that leverage existing numerical frameworks, leading the way for breakthroughs in simulating active galaxies through gas dynamics simulations. The increasing number of IoT devices being used in various settings, such as sports venues, has led to growing concerns about IoT-based malware spreading and potential system vulnerabilities. Current methods for testing IoT applications are time-consuming and often ineffective, blocking the development of new technologies and hindering the adoption of research findings. To address this issue, the authors introduce the Frisbee framework, a pioneering approach for automatically generating and executing precise and complex tests on IoT applications. By leveraging the existing virtues of the HaViMoPath model and the TGraph algorithm, Frisbee identifies intricate attack paths and converts them into usable test cases. Its unique capabilities make Frisbee an invaluable tool for enhancing the testing process of IoT applications and, as such, it is offered as an open-source platform for researchers and developers to utilize and contribute to. Furthermore, a demonstration of the framework's functionality can be viewed by accessing the accompanying video. In addition to its practical uses, Frisbee also facilitates collaborations among researchers, shaping the future of IoT security testing and paving the way for further advancements in the field. As part of its suite of features, the framework includes a sophisticated attack path generation algorithm and a graphical user interface, both of which have been openly available since December 2023 on the Zenodo repository, reference [1]. The underlying HaViMoPath model and the innovative approach of Frisbee have been publicly disclosed only in this research paper. In its current iteration, the framework is capable of simulating up to 30 HaViMoPath models concurrently and executing cross-protocol attacks. The development team is now working on its next iteration, code-named "GrafX", which is an open-source project that can be found on GitHub, reference [2]. The authors invite feedback, suggestions, and contributions from the research community to help them refine and expand the capabilities of the Frisbee framework. The technology behind this work has been independently validated and its contributors have been highlighted in the added text. The work described in this paper has been funded by the National Science Foundation, grant number 1738094, which focused on investigating the security challenges associated with IoT applications in sports settings. As part of this research, a comprehensive survey on IoT security was conducted and the results have been included in the paper's appendix. The findings from this study have been factored into the development of the HaViMoMoPath model and the subsequent attack path generation algorithm. The research presented in this paper has been presented at two high-profile conferences: the 2023 IEEE/AC

New limitations on the rate of rare B meson decays were set by the LHCb experiment in 2012, using data from 35 pb^-1 of 7 TeV proton-proton collisions at the LHC. These rate limitations were based on two specific decay processes: B^0_s to mu+ mu- and B^0 to mu+ mu-. The first of these rare decays was found to occur at a rate that was 5.4 standard deviations different from the predicted value set by the Standard Model, while the second was within expected limits. Additionally, LHCb experiments in 2015 and 2016, using up to 3 fb^-1 of 7 and 8 TeV data respectively, narrowed the rate differences for B^0_s to mu+ mu- and B^0 to mu+ mu- to their predicted Standard Model values, but at rates that were slightly elevated and required further verification. When combining all available 7 and 8 TeV data (3 fb^-1), a rate difference of 2.1 standard deviations from the expected value was found for B^0_s to mu+ mu-, while B^0 to mu+ mu- remained within expected limits. These findings contribute to a broader understanding of rare B meson decays and could indicate the presence of new physics phenomena. While further research is needed to verify these discoveries, they pave the way for even more precise measurements in the search for rare B meson decays at the LHC in upcoming data sets from the LHC at higher energy levels. The current findings were based on analyses developed before 2015 and resulted in rate limitations on the decay process B^0_s to mu+ mu- that were 5.4 standard deviations different from the predicted value set by the Standard Model, and on combining all available 7 and 8 TeV data (3 fb^-1), a rate difference of 2.1 standard deviations from the expected value was found for B^0_s to mu+ mu-. The findings on B^0 to mu+ mu- remained within expected limits at a rate difference of 0.7 standard deviations from the predicted value set by the Standard Model. Current approaches to training autonomous vehicles using real-world data focus on generating entire scenes, but often prioritize visual variety over practical relevance. This limitation hinders the development of a robust training regimen. To address this issue, we introduce SceneGen, a method that gradationally increases scene complexity to mimic the natural progression of scenes encountered during normal driving. SceneGen undergoes extensive evaluation, demonstrating its capacity to create challenging scenes that surpass previous methods and bridge the gap between synthetic and real scenes. Furthermore, we show that SceneGen can be employed within a training framework that prioritizes diversity and scene complexity, resulting in a 10% improvement in lane change detection. Additionally, we observe a 5% reduction in false positives and a 10% improvement in lane change prediction. To facilitate progress in this area, we release both SceneGen and the evaluation toolkit as open-source resources. These advancements and resulting tools are expected to facilitate the development of sophisticated scene modeling methods and accelerate the training of autonomous vehicles using real-world data. They can be found at the accompanying website https://scengen.autowriters.com/.

In the context of Cayley trees, we develop an exact cluster expansion for the Ising model, enabling the derivation of cluster weight factors through group representation theory. This approach results in a novel explicit formula for the partition function, which can be computed efficiently for any Cayley tree structure. We leverage this framework to examine the Ising model on a Cayley tree in the canonical ensemble, focusing particularly on the effects of temperature on the partition function, cumulant expansion, and magnetic field calculations. Moreover, we demonstrate that our method may be applied to analyze other lattice models by considering examples of the Potts model and an SU(2) Heisenberg model. Notably, our results reveal intriguing patterns of convergence for the partition function and its derivatives as the inverse temperature increases, characterized by power-law behavior before eventually converging to a minimum at a critical temperature. The proposed method offers a versatile numerical tool for studying lattice models on Cayley trees and related graph structures. Several theoretical and numerical aspects of our approach are also discussed. This research introduces an innovative iteration method, specifically a generalized
version of the Flexible Galerkinized Minimal Residual Square (FGMRES) iteration, utilized
to solve time-dependent partial differential equations. The proposed iteration method
incorporates an explicit approximation of the operator, addressing an inherent limitation
of the standard FGMRES method. The new iteration method is mathematically defined
and statistically analyzed in terms of its convergence rate and computational cost.
Numerical experiments are conducted to demonstrate the method's effectiveness and
convergent performance on a range of models, including the advection-diffusion equation,
the Navier-Stokes equations, and the Klein-Gordon equation. The results are compared
against a range of established iterative methods, further highlighting the method's
advantages. All numerical experiments were performed using the publicly available
finite element framework DOLFIN, developed by the FEniCS Project. The framework's
python interface, specifically the 'fem' and 'fempy' modules, was leveraged to
implement and evaluate the novel FGMRES method. The implementation and associated
code are made publicly accessible through the COMSOL GitHub repository. The study
concludes that the proposed fixed-scale FGMRES (fsFGMRES) method generally converges
quadratically, outperforming the standard FGMRES method and several alternative
iterative methods across diverse test cases. The fsFGMRES method is characterized
by its simplicity and minimal additional computational overhead. The research suggests
that the fixed-scale fsFGMRES method can be an effective strategy for accelerating
convergent iterative methods, particularly for challenging problems requiring
high-precision solutions. The proposed fixed-scale fsFGMRES method is an attractive
alternative to complex multi-level correction techniques and other advanced methods. 
The study's results can be further improved through the use of more sophisticated
operator approximations, leading to potential applications across a broader spectrum
of problems. The implementation of the fixed-scale fsFGMRES method can be extended
to encompass a broader range of iterative methods, such as the GMRES method, by
switching between different iteration methods based on the solution phase. The study
concludes that the fixed-scale fsFGMRES method is an efficient and effective tool
for accelerating the convergence of numerical solutions to partial differential equations.

code within the COMSOL GitHub repository. The study's results are deemed globally

Our analysis reveals that this condition leads to the convergence of ergodic averages along specific sequences indexed by square roots. In addition, we demonstrate that systems lacking joint ergodicity dynamics may exhibit non-convergent averages for certain polynomials. Our results address two significant open problems, providing a comprehensive solution to Problem 6.1 and offering a partial solution to Problem 6.2 within the realm of compact group extensions of solenoids. Moreover, our findings yield novel equidistribution statements for ergodic measures on orbit sets within these systems, yielding improvements to previous results. Moreover, we establish the non-convergent nature of ergodic averages for certain systems that have been identified by Iosif on several distinct sequences indexed by powers of highly composite numbers. Consequently, our investigation resolves open problems 5.1, 6.1, and 6.2 entirely, and partially resolves problem 5.2.
