A new framework for unsupervised pre-training is introduced, comprising two critical components: a method for generating pseudo segmentations and a set of logical rules governing data consistency. This approach, called Uniscope, seeks to develop high-quality pseudo segmentations that conform to the data consistency principles by employing a probabilistic graphical model called PCMHM. Unlike existing approaches, Uniscope's framework and method are designed to improve upon existing pseudo segmentations through mutual enhancement. This is achieved by modeling the interdependencies between pseudo segmentations and incorporating them into the PCMHM model. Consequently, Uniscope yields more accurate results across multiple medical segmentation tasks compared to alternative unsupervised methods. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through improvements to three public datasets and a comparative analysis of the proposed approach over multiple trials. The source code and benchmark results are available online.

Understanding why other players' actions succeed or fail is crucial for achieving goals in complex cooperative scenarios. By incorporating a theory-of-mind approach, agents can utilize their inferences about other agents' intentions and beliefs to guide their own decision-making. Despite the potential benefits, traditional methods of cognitive modeling, such as planning-based and imitation learning approaches, often face significant challenges. To address these issues, we introduce a new algorithm that leverages mental state modeling to enhance its own performance. In a collaborative game setting, this approach enables an agent to estimate the effects of its actions on the other players' intentions and learn a value function that considers these inferences. Through evaluation results, we show that the algorithm can effectively learn from scratch and achieve better goal achievement rates compared to baseline methods, such as state-sharing, action-modeling agents. While previous research focused mainly on context-based approaches, this work proposes an alternative strategy, leveraging the vast amount of labeled data available to identify and explain changes in word meanings. We examine the concept of semantic shift and categorize it into three types: enrichment, transformation, and loss of meaning. To tackle this task, we used a combination of retrieval-based and generative methods to develop models that could learn from large language datasets and label words as semantically rich, evolving, or lost their meaning. Evaluating these models on a newly created dataset containing 10,000 words with labeled semantic shift properties showed they performed better than baseline models and could detect words with shifting meanings significantly more effectively than models that weren't fine-tuned on this task. This indicates that large language models possess an inherent ability to recognize words with changing meanings and that fine-tuning them makes them even more accurate at identifying these words. Moreover, our results revealed that generative models were more skilled at detecting words with shifting meanings and contextualized models within the retrieval-based group. This research lays the groundwork for an interesting area of study on the capabilities and limitations of language models in grasping semantic shift and will contribute to the development of more sophisticated models that can capture the complexities of language evolution. The data and techniques we presented in this paper will be useful for other research projects involving the evaluation of LMs on semantic shift properties. The primary challenge in this research remains the scarcity of labeled data, which can be addressed by crowdsourcing large-scale datasets annotated with semantic shift properties. In this paper, we initiated this exploration by crowdsourcing our initial dataset. The most substantial contribution we made was developing a labeling framework consisting of multiple stages that ensured the quality and reliability of the annotations collected. This approach involved sequential and concurrent stages of candidate selection, review, and revision stages conducted by increasingly specialized annotators aimed at decreasing the workload burden and the number of annotations required. The techniques we used to manage this process allowed us to collect 10,000 word labels with shift properties in just over three months, something that wouldn't have been possible without these efficient methods that boosted annotation speed and quality by at least 1.5 times in a series of carefully managed experiments involving multiple, independent annotator teams. These functions demonstrate a strong correlation between the transverse positions of quarks within a hadron and exhibit symptoms of quark localization increasing with the confinement force between quarks. The uncertainty in the quark localization, for instance, was found to be around one sigma ($\sigma \approx 0.15$ fm) when considering the minimal simulation uncertainties. Understanding protein folding is crucial to analyzing protein function and sequence-based predictions. Knotted proteins pose a high challenge due to their complex structures. We introduce a new method to simulate deep and shallow protein knot folding in silico. By examining various starting conditions and simulations of over 100 test cases, we found that shallow knots tend to fold through a single pathway, in contrast to deep knots which can fold via multiple paths. The proposed algorithm successfully predicted structures consistent with experimentally verified knot types and folding routes. Additionally, our method demonstrated better performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods. We suggest that knot folding can be studied at different temperature levels to distinguish between shallow and deep knots. Mainland China has over 560 million netizens, making it one of the most connected populations in the world. Due to extensive online activities, there is a growing need for online user data, particularly with rising concerns about privacy. To address the challenges of collecting high-quality multi-label data, we introduce a novel sampling approach called single-to-multi-label (S2M) sampling, which significantly reduces annotation costs by a factor of $n$ compared to traditional methods. We utilize S2M sampling to gather an extensive dataset consisting of 1 million product titles annotated with prices, with one annotation used for each sample instead of the traditional method of using multiple annotations for the same data sample. We also develop a comprehensive study involving three well-known zero-shot multi-label text classification models, incorporating a novel evaluation protocol to assess model performance. Our research demonstrates that the models learn from S2M samples and actual labeling costs, with notable improvements in accuracy due to the reduced noise from S2M sampling. Moreover, we observe substantial savings in annotation costs without sacrificing model efficacy. To facilitate replication and advancement of current models dealing with low-cost multi-label data collection, we release our code and dataset publicly available at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/EasyMLTC. 

Key contributions of this study include:
* Introducing single-to-multi-label (S2M) sampling, a novel, cost-effective data collection method reducing annotation costs by a factor of n for multi-label data.
* Developing a comprehensive dataset of product titles with prices, where each annotation represents a label.
* Creating a comprehensive evaluation framework for zero-shot multi-label text classification models that learn from S2M samples and actual labeling costs.
* Demonstrating notable improvements in model accuracy due to the reduced noise from S2M sampling, resulting in significant annotation cost savings without compromising model efficacy.
* Making the code and dataset available publicly at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/EasyMLTC to facilitate replication and advancement of current models dealing with low-cost multi-label data collection.

It builds on the Fama-French model by incorporating four key factors and uses a broad dataset of US stocks. The model demonstrates a clear structure for organizing stocks within a specific portfolio based on the returns of a particular asset class, providing detailed estimates of expected returns and risk levels for each subset of stocks. The increasing use of wearable devices for real-time health monitoring has raised concerns over maintaining user privacy. This has led to a growing interest in developing privacy-preserving deep learning techniques for mobile devices. Our research, FedHealth, focuses on creating a federated framework for training deep learning models on wearable devices that recognize physical activities using accelerometer data. Unlike conventional models that rely on data similarity, FedHealth uses a unique approach where each device trains a separate model using local data and then shares the model with the server for updates. The server processes the models from each device, identifying any similarities or differences, and uses this information to update the model for each device. This led to a significant 12.5% improvement in accuracy and 10.2% reduction in loss compared to traditional federated learning approaches. This research investigates the impact of an underlying diffusion on options, specifically looking at the effect of barrier features. To analyze this, we utilize backward stochastic differential equations, which can model a range of financial derivatives, including options with knock-in/knock-out barriers. To tackle this problem, an additional strategy is employed where a new asset is introduced to represent the change in the equation's coefficients, this then enables us to apply the method of fundamental solutions to solve the equations. Through numerical experiments, it becomes clear that even a small underlying diffusion can significantly raise options' values, also note that in some cases, this effect can be viewed as additive with other factors affecting options' values. Furthermore, different types of barrier features can lead to non-predictable behavior in options' values, this is demonstrated through a detailed analysis of a European call option with a knock-in barrier. To model options with time-dependent barriers, a modification of the standard BSE approach is required, this involves applying a change of measure, this leads to a solvable BSE equation, however for options with barriers that depend on multiple assets, this approach fails, this is shown through a model involving two assets, this model results in a system of BSE equations, that cannot be solved for an explicit formula. This research also compares the performance of different numerical methods for solving BSE equations, this includes the method of fundamental solutions, a Monte-Carlo approach, and a regression-based method, it is shown that the method of fundamental solutions outperforms the other methods in terms of computational time, this is demonstrated through solving a BSE equation with multiple assets. Finally, this research is applicable to real-world financial derivative products, this is illustrated through an example of a European call option with a knock-in barrier, this option is based on an asset price model known as the Heston model. This research also provides a theoretical analysis of how options prices behave under different regimes of an underlying asset's volatility, this is achieved by solving the BSE equation for an explicit formula in a particular case, this involves applying a change of measure, this results in a geometric Brownian motion with a different volatility parameter, this then enables us to apply the method of fundamental solutions to solve the equation. Through this approach, it is possible to derive an explicit formula for options prices in different regimes of volatility, this includes deriving the optimal payoff in different regimes of volatility, this is achieved by applying the method of fundamental solutions to a system of ordinary differential equations, this system is derived from the BSE equation. Theoretical leptoquark pair production in an asymmetric scenario has been mathematically quantified in a comprehensive manner and its relevance in current and future experiments evaluated. This analysis, valid across various colliders including PDF-dependent ones like the Tevatron and Atlas/CMS, and PDF-agnostic ones like ILC, CLIC, and future leptoquark colliders, focuses on asymptotic, kinetically dominant processes to derive unifying, closure approximated cross-section formulas applicable across various new physics scales. Empirical thresholds, spin effects, and logarithmic dependencies at the production level are accounted for in these formulas, which can also be employed to determine relevant detection channels, exploit natural suppression factors, and pinpoint relevant reconstruction tools. By leveraging these formulas, potential production regions of the Tevatron and CMS can be re-evaluated or refined, potentially revealing hidden leptoquark production regions. Moreover, they provide a foundation for adapting existing experimental analysis code to model leptoquark behavior in various colliders. As a result, a publicly accessible code package called 'ASYMQUARK' is now available to model this production process and associated decay pathways for various leptoquark types and decay channels. In addition, it includes a set of cross-section formulas for reference. The package also enables the simulation of detector responses to various leptoquark scenarios, enabling the direct comparison of theoretical predictions with experimental data. As a demonstration, several theoretical production region predictions are compared with existing Tevatron and CMS experiments' results. The code can be modified to accommodate new production regions or feedback is welcome to further enhance its capabilities. The theoretical production region predictions made by 'ASYMQUARK' can be viewed within the package as well as on the Hep-Ude website dedicated to leptoquark research. The code and research platform are regularly updated to reflect the latest theoretical and experimental developments. The extension of this work to other production processes or non-collinear scenarios is also feasible with the developed framework. The package 'ASYMQUARK' is now available at https://github.com/udehxu/ASYMQUARK. The research underlying this work has been presented in several talks at the 2021 Leptoquark Collider Workshop and the 2022 Fundamental Particle Physics Workshop. The associated slides can be found on the workshop websites. Accurately identifying genes with predictive power for patient outcomes from time-dependent gene expression data remains a complex challenge for biomedical researchers. Despite the success of machine learning in this area, there are significant drawbacks to applying these models in a wide range of settings. Models are often slow to train, require a substantial amount of data, and result in inconsistent selections of predictive genes. To address these limitations, we present a novel algorithm called RelevanceMatcher, a model-agnostic method for efficient predictive variable discovery. By incorporating a separate relevance learning module, RelevanceMatcher identifies key variables quickly and with minimal data, allowing the primary model to focus on efficient training. We demonstrate the performance of RelevanceMatcher, incorporating an efficient neural network, on real-world datasets showcasing a significant reduction in training time and test error compared to existing solutions. The algorithm's code is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/yin-yang-lab/RelevanceMatcher.

Highly intense starburst galaxies often exhibit unusual Circumgalactic Medium reservoirs, which can influence their surrounding environment through mass excision. This study investigates the relationship between these reservoirs and the galaxies' C IV and H beta Emission Line Ratios, which indicate the presence of molecular wind patterns or gas reservoirs, particularly in regions around galaxies known as "twin Teos". By analyzing spectra from the Hubble Space Telescope, we found significant variations in our test sample of 11 galaxies. Although they exhibit similar spectra, our data shows distinct variations in the galaxies' C IV and H beta Emission Line Ratios, which do not correlate with other galaxy characteristics. This suggests a possible connection to the massive starbursts' potential for shaping their surroundings through mass loss. However, our findings also indicate that this process might take longer than 400 million years to have a significant impact on the galaxies' C IV and H beta Emission Line Ratios. This study provides valuable insights into the galaxies' interactions with their surroundings and suggests potential markers for identifying galaxies with extensive starbursts. Moreover, it lays the groundwork for using high-resolution spectra to study galaxies known as "Dwarf Quasistar galaxies" and analyze how they manage their massive energy outputs. This research could help answer questions about how these galaxies accelerate particles, shape their surroundings, and potentially produce Fast Radio Bursts. Ultimately, this study paves the way for a deeper understanding of the unique properties and behaviors of extreme starburst galaxies, which could shed light on the fundamental nature of these galaxies and their significant energy outputs. The high accuracy of commercial Question Answering (QA) systems can be misleading, especially for users who are not tech-savvy and rely on search engines for information. This research addresses this issue by introducing the QASPER dataset, which contains inappropriate explanations intentionally crafted to mislead people into believing a certain fact is true. These misleading explanations were designed to be convincing and were used to trick QA systems into generating false conclusions. Based on the BART model, we developed a method to enhance the accuracy of QA systems by incorporating a secondary task that helps them distinguish between accurate and misleading explanations. This approach led to a significant improvement in the models' performance on the QASPER dataset, showing they could better handle the challenging task of identifying misleading explanations. Notably, our experiments revealed that simply training the models on existing QA datasets did not prepare them for dealing with misleading explanations, implying that special training is required to tackle this issue. Additionally, our approach prompted discussions on the potential applications of models that can model risks, such as those related to the spread of false information. Furthermore, our method demonstrated an interesting benefit of generating answers with higher accuracy even when presented with misleading explanations, which could be useful for improving QA systems in real-world scenarios. Overall, our work introduced an innovative method for evaluating and improving the ability of QA systems to resist the impact of misleading information and also provided an opportunity for exploring other potential uses and implications. As a result, the research community now has access to the QASPER dataset, which is a valuable tool for advancing the state of the art in QA systems and opening new paths for investigating other risk-related topics. This research ultimately aimed to take a crucial step in addressing the challenge of providing users with reliable information by helping QA systems become more resilient to misleading information and capable of effectively identifying unnecessary explanations. In doing so, it also shed light on the potential applications of models that focus on modeling risks and highlighted the need for further exploration into this newly initiated topic. In conclusion, the introduction of the QASPER dataset has the potential to contribute significantly to the development of more dependable and socially responsible QA systems that can minimize the diffusion of false information and be an important step towards a future where machines can model risks for the betterment of humanity. This research has numerous avenues for further exploration and hopefully, these findings will spark new interest in evaluating and enhancing the social responsibility of language models. We investigate the velocity set $\mathcal{V}_k(t)$ of the $k$-th particle from the right in ASEP with initial data specified by the discrete step function on the integers. We demonstrate that the velocity distribution at time $t$ can be represented as a probability ratio $\frac{1}{2t+1}$, where velocities within the range $[-1,1]$ are proportional to $\frac{1}{2t+1}$ and velocities outside this range are proportional to $\frac{2t+1}{1}$.

We also examine the asymptotic distribution of $\mathcal{V}_k(t)$ as $t$ approaches infinity. It is observed that for $k$ less than $1-t$ and greater than $-1+t$, the probability of being in a stationary state at time $t$ follows an odd function of $\frac{k-t}{t}$.

Furthermore, we express the $k$-th particle from the right in ASEP as being in one of two different hydrodynamic regimes. It is shown that for $k$ greater than $-1+t$ and less than $1-t$, the system can be viewed as having a shock wave with speed $k$ and probability distribution proportional to $\frac{1+(k-1)t}{1+(1-k)t}$. Mathematical models of disease transmission play a crucial role in evaluating pandemic control measures and estimating the effectiveness of vaccination strategies. However, most existing models overlook critical aspects of model selection, such as feasibility, that are fundamental to both mathematical and biological frameworks. In this study, we address this limitation by developing a method to evaluate disease models that considers both feasibility and consistency with observed data. Our approach involves using optimization techniques to identify the model parameters that best fit the data and meet the feasibility requirements. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method by applying it to a series of realistic epidemic models, including one related to the recent SARS-CoV-2 pandemic. Our results show that even models with inherently flawed assumptions can fit the data reasonably well; nevertheless, these models fail to meet basic feasibility standards and are unlikely to be biologically plausible. Interestingly, the parameters that fit the data are often associated with model behaviors that are both feasible and data-fitting; we refer to such parameters as "coherent" parameters. Our research suggests that simply accepting the best-fit model parameters without considering feasibility may lead to incorrect conclusions. In the context of the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, our results indicate that the current vaccination strategy may fail to prevent future epidemics on its own, prompting the need for an alternative perspective on this issue. Our study paves the way for a more comprehensive reevaluation of disease models that integrates mathematical and biological insights. Moreover, our method is versatile and can be adapted to accommodate model learning within dynamic frameworks, such as the sequential model selection approach. By reconciling mathematical and biological feasibility, our approach offers a valuable framework for a more nuanced understanding of complex systems and the implications they have for the environment and control systems. This research addresses the challenges of acronym identification and disambiguation in natural language, which typically stem from the limited and unclear definition of acronyms. This problem is compounded by the vast and diverse nature of writing systems, which includes differences in case, punctuation, and spelling. To tackle this issue, we propose a multi-stage approach employing machine learning algorithms and a data structure called a suffix tree. Initially, we leverage character n-grams and text classification to identify potential acronyms based on their formatting. Next, we employ the suffix tree to analyze the text and determine the likelihood of each identified acronym corresponding to a specific sequence of characters. We tested our approach on two datasets containing colloquial expressions and scientific citations, which demonstrated our system's capacity to accurately identify acronyms in 95% of cases and disambiguate them in 90% of instances. Furthermore, our approach has the potential to be enhanced for various writing domains with the incorporation of additional systems that can learn from data and incorporate domain-specific knowledge. Additionally, we observed that our method is robust in addressing acronyms with unclear definitions and those part of longer phrases. The code for our approach has been made publicly accessible to support the further development of acronym disambiguation. The potential for incorporating contextual grammar into our approach is also explored in this research. The techniques introduced in this research have the potential to be applied to other challenges involving unclear writing, such as deciphering handwritten text. In contrast, the paper [] proposes a new way to build deinterlacing networks with compact, direct training on raw video frames. Moreover, the proposed approach includes two novel models: one that directly converts interlaced video to bitmap, and another that first converts video to progressive frames before transforming them into bitmap. Determining the density distribution of neutrons in the outside layer of nuclear matter is an important goal. This information can be used to understand the relationship between the density of neutrons and the potential energy that influences nucleon properties within the nucleus. A novel method of investigation has been developed that utilizes longitudinal form factors of nuclear monopoles to study the density distribution of neutrons. By analyzing the root mean square values of these form factors in various nuclei, researchers found a strong correlation between neutron density and charge density at the center of the nucleus. Furthermore, a separate analysis of data showed a clear relationship between the density of neutrons at the outside layer of the nucleus and the potential energy that influences nucleon properties. From the current understanding, it appears that the density of neutrons in the outside layer of the nucleus is higher when the density of protons is lower than average, as researchers found in previous studies. This effect holds true for light and intermediate mass nuclei but breaks down for heavy mass nuclei where proton clusters play a significant role. A theoretical calculation based on the neutron skin thickness also revealed a linear relationship between the density of neutrons in the outside layer of the nucleus and the potential energy that influences nucleon properties, often referred to as the symmetry potential. This research provides significant new insights into the properties of nuclear matter and suggests that the density of neutrons in the outside layer of the nucleus is highly sensitive to the presence of protons within the nucleus. As a result, the thickness of the neutron skin can be a powerful probe for future deep underground neutrino detectors that need to be deeply understood and accurately predicted through detailed theoretical and experimental research. In conclusion, this study underscores the importance of precisely measuring the density distribution of neutrons in the outside layer of nuclear matter, especially in heavy mass nuclei such as neutron stars. This knowledge can be used to understand the relationship between the density of neutrons and the potential energy that influences nucleon properties within the nucleus. In addition, a deeper comprehension of this relationship will provide valuable new insights into the properties of nuclear matter, especially in heavy mass nuclei such as neutron stars that are shrouded in mystery. While researchers have made significant progress in the past, there is still a significant need for detailed theoretical and experimental research to accurately predict the thickness of the neutron skin in heavy mass nuclei such as neutron stars. Specifically, it has been localized in the context of simplicial sets within the context of motivic stable homotopy theory. This localization enables the application of the b-principle to motivic problems. Moreover, it yields a motivic version of the Madsen-Weiss theorem. This paper provides conditions under which the symmetric matrix $X$ has a spectral distribution that exists in probability or almost surely. The matrix $X$ is defined as the sum of an independent, symmetric, random variable $a_{ij}$, with at least two different possible values. Additionally, this work offers a direct approach to identifying the matrix $X$'s spectral distribution through a single, self-consistent equation. This method can be applied to matrices with correlated or dependent entries. A specific technique is also introduced for generating an approximate, non-rigid autoregressive process using a matrix with a predetermined spectral distribution. This technique can be applied to any type of matrix, including those with correlated or dependent entries. A direct approach is also provided for generating an autoregressive process that corresponds to a given spectral distribution. A corollary of this method can be used to create approximate, non-rigid ARMA processes. A new algorithm is also introduced for estimating the unknown parameters $f_X$ of a matrix $X$ that are related to its spectral distribution. This algorithm is based on a direct, "closed-form" approach for identifying the spectral distribution of $X$. It is designed to work efficiently with large, complex matrices. A specific application of this algorithm is the development of an alternative method for estimating the large-sample spectral distribution of $X$. This new method outperforms existing methods, such as the unbiased estimator $\frac{1}{n}Tr(\hat{f}_n)$, especially for large, complex matrices. A specific advantage of this algorithm is its ability to handle "rigid" matrices, such as Toeplitz or block-Toeplitz matrices. A condition is established under which the estimated spectral distribution $\hat{f}_{X_n}$ converges to the true spectral distribution $f_X$ in probability or almost surely. This condition is based on the properties of the matrix $X$ and its entries. It does not rely on any assumptions about the matrix $X$ being positive definite or non-singular. A specific approach is also introduced for identifying the matrix $X$'s spectral distribution when a specific class of symmetric, independent, and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables are used to define the matrix $X$. This approach can be applied to any type of matrix with i.i.d. entries. It provides a direct and simple way to identify the matrix $X$'s spectral distribution. Persuasive videos aim to influence viewers' opinions, often incorporating engaging background music to capture their attention.
We introduce a novel approach to automate background music creation for these videos, ensuring the generated soundtracks align with the intended perspective.
Our method leverages a music-generation tool, specifically Tailor, and refines the output to match the visual content and promote perspective-aware listening.
Initial results indicate that human evaluators prefer the generated music over a baseline approach, although further improvements are needed to achieve similar listening experiences as perspective-aware videos intended for human audiences.
Our approach demonstrates potential for background music generation in persuasive visual-audio data, requiring larger datasets to yield comparable results to current state-of-the-art methods.

Furthermore, the underlying assumption of most existing evaluations is flawed, as it presumes that gradient masking can be reliable and consistent across diverse models. In order to enhance evaluation flexibility and align with the assumption that gradient masking is inherently unstable, we've developed a quantitative metric called gradient masking index (gmi). The gmi assesses the likelihood of model behaviors in relation to gradient masking. In addition, we've introduced a novel procedure for training neural networks that allows for control over the gradient masking index. This training method can yield models that either consistently mask or consistently do not mask gradients. Based on these new developments, we've conducted a series of experiments, including a comparison of models that differ in their gradient masking indices. Our findings indicate that models with higher gmi scores exhibit improved security against various attack methods, as evaluated through both metrics of success and confidence. As a result, we're able to draw a crucial distinction between two distinct behaviors in neural networks: gradient masking and noise robustness. In relation to prior work, our research has significant implications, given that many studies based trust in the consistency of gradient masking. Consequently, we propose that all future research should prioritize control of the gmi when training models that employ gradient masking. We investigate how non-linear standard assumptions of Gaussian diffusion can be challenged by diverse forms of correlations and heterogeneity present in complex networks. A distinct class of network models is considered here, characterized by uncorrelated and heterogeneous diffusing particles. Our analysis reveals that such models consistently exhibit non-Gaussian behavior at all scales of observation. The reasons for non-Gaussianity in this context can be attributed to two factors: the network's structure and the starting conditions of the diffusion process. Specific network architectures can lead to the emergence of power-law, exponential, or skewed distributions among the observed node values. Moreover, the network's correlation profile transitions from heterogeneity-driven to heterogeneity-free as the diffusion parameter increases, resulting in notable deviations from power-law behavior. Our research provides a thorough examination of the effects of correlations and heterogeneity on Gaussian diffusion models, offering insights that can be applied to various complex systems and leading to the proposal of a general framework for analyzing non-linear, network-based diffusion processes. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of our approach to real-world scenarios, including the study of financial network stability and the analysis of physical and biological systems that involve random searches. Alongside its network-focused contributions, our research also paves the way for a broader exploration of complex systems characterized by time-varying and non-linear dynamics. In this sense, our findings are expected to yield valuable insights into the fundamental properties and behaviors of a wide range of network-based systems. Our study is accompanied by a publicly accessible code to facilitate the simulation of our proposed models and the associated data analysis. By combining theoretical and computational approaches, our research offers a comprehensive framework that is instrumental in uncovering the intricate dynamics governing complex network-based systems. Despite their similar generation mechanisms, the strength of cross-phase modulation surpasses that of self-phase modulation. This phenomenon can be understood by considering the relative speeds of the counterpropagating waves and the change in phase of the light within the loop. As a result of the speed difference, cross-phase modulation affects one wave over a longer distance than self-phase modulation, thereby increasing its strength. To demonstrate this effect, a loop resonator consisting of a $1.5$ um micrometer was constructed, allowing the temperature-controlled generation of cross-phase and self-phase modulation in opposing waves with differing speeds. The resulting four-wave mixing products showed the desired increase in cross-phase modulation-related signals in the hotter sections and the desired decrease in self-phase modulation-related signals in the cooler sections, thus demonstrating the potential of this phenomenon for enhanced frequency conversion efficiency in loop resonators. This research involves enhancing super-resolution GAN models using multiscale techniques, with the objective of creating highly realistic, high-resolution images of turbulent flow velocity profiles. Despite prior research demonstrating the promise of this approach, the models' reliability depends on testing beyond the scope of the training data, specifically under varying flow conditions represented by different Reynolds numbers. To address this issue, we train and evaluate several multiscale GAN models using direct numerical simulation data of turbulent channel flow at Reynolds numbers 180 and 3200. The evaluation involves comparing the performance of these models in predicting high-resolution images of turbulent flow velocity profiles at Reynolds numbers 55, 180, 3200, and 5500. The results show that a single-model approach fails to accurately predict velocity profiles across all Reynolds numbers tested. In contrast, a multiscale approach yields more realistic predictions and demonstrates a level of detail that is consistent with the level of turbulence it is trained on. Ultimately, our findings validate the potential of deep learning models like GAN to produce highly detailed, high-fidelity simulations of turbulent flow velocity profiles. Moreover, our analysis provides insights into the performance of these models and suggests that their accuracy depends on the level of turbulence they are trained on and tested against. While this research involves turbulent channel flow, the findings may have implications for similar deep learning applications in other complex fluid dynamics scenarios. Additionally, this work sets the stage for exploring other deep learning architectures and enhancing the models' ability to predict flow velocity profiles across all Reynolds numbers without training data specific to each condition. By doing so, we aim to leverage the immense computational power of modern deep learning models to create highly accurate, high-resolution simulations of turbulent flow velocity profiles, even in complex geometries. In this research, we achieve this goal by training a single-model, high-resolution simulator using a massive dataset of turbulent channel flow velocity profiles at a Reynolds number of 180. The resulting model produces remarkably realistic predictions across all Reynolds numbers tested, including those not included in the training data. In the future, this approach may enable the development of highly accurate, high-resolution simulations of turbulent flow conditions, including those that involve changes in flow geometry, multi-phase flow, and external flow scenarios. In these scenarios, combining deep learning models with traditional numerical methods for solving partial differential equations may provide a more feasible approach. This work lays the groundwork for exploring this integrated approach to developing novel deep learning-based numerical methods that can accurately solve complex fluid dynamics problems. Deep neural network classifiers have revolutionized the field of computer vision by achieving near-human performance on various tasks, but they are prone to making misleading predictions with high confidence levels when classifying images intended for out-of-domain categories. This issue arises because traditional deep learning training methods prioritize optimizing the model's accuracy and confidence in predicting the training dataset over everything else. In contrast, human experts are not only accurate in their predictions but also tend to be uncertain when predicting categories outside their experience domain. This research explores the concept of uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks and presents an innovative training approach called Relative Confidence Enhancement (RCE). The RCE framework learns to differentiate between predictive confidence and uncertainty by introducing an iterative learning algorithm that adjusts the loss function to penalize excessive confidence in prediction tasks. The algorithm amplifies the model's confidence in predicted categories by increasing the learning rate, and it slows down the learning rate in cases of uncertain predictions. This research provides an RCE implementation for both regression and multi-class classification tasks and showcases its effectiveness with an image classification example involving an intended out-of-domain category. Experimental results indicate that RCE-enhanced deep neural networks can effectively differentiate between prediction confidence and uncertainty, leading to more realistic uncertainty quantification. Furthermore, this research explores various quantification methods for measuring uncertainty, including reliability depth and prediction distribution entropy. The findings suggest that RCE can learn to recognize uncertain predictions even without additional uncertainty data. The proposed framework addresses two prominent issues in deep neural networks: overconfidence and uncertainty quantification. We suggest a new evaluation framework for reinforcement learning algorithms that learn from a stream of curriculum changes, allowing us to systematically modify learning conditions and assess the credit assignment capabilities of each algorithm. Our framework leads to a clear mathematical definition of curriculum control and objective evaluation metrics that reflect the ability of each algorithm to leverage changes in the curriculum. We apply our approach to a fundamental gridworld example, where we investigate the impact of different curriculum strategies and evaluation metrics on the performance of reinforcement learning algorithms, including both hierarchical and flat architectures. Our findings demonstrate that neural network-based algorithms excel in responding to curriculum changes, whereas linear function approximation methods struggle to adapt to shifting reward optimization objectives. The results also reveal the advantages of hierarchical reinforcement learning methods in overcoming curriculum obstacles and efficiently exploring environments. Ultimately, our work highlights the significance of curriculum control in evaluating reinforcement learning algorithms and paves the way for further research into the design of effective learning conditions and evaluation criteria. The source code for our experiments is available online.

This phenomenon of localization and delocalization can be understood by studying a single-mode system. By analyzing a single resonator in an infinite array of interacting cavities, particularly those based on the Cantor set, we found that there is a critical point where a mode's localization transitions from a distant to a nearest-neighbor distribution. This critical point is influenced by the system's self-leakage and synchronization properties and can be adjusted through changes in the cavity's internal loss, its coupling to nearby cavities, and changes in the cavity's resonance frequency. These findings can also be applied to other similar systems. Moreover, our analysis reveals that these systems exhibit a type of bi-stability. This means that for specific conditions, there are two possible localization states and both can be created through controlled variations in the system's parameters. Liger is a cutting-edge, multi-messenger gravitational wave detector consisting of two kilometer-long interferometers located in the Hanford and Livingston sites in the United States. Liger's sensitivity and capabilities will be enhanced through the use of advanced signal-processing technologies, including the Data Reduction System (DRS). The DRS system comprises numerous interconnected components, including data reduction networks and data storage systems, protected from potential faults by error-correcting codes. A significant aspect of the DRS system involves anomaly detection software that is designed to promptly shut down the system in the event of suspected errors. Although this detection system can minimize the likelihood of unforeseen malfunctions, it cannot eliminate the risk of errors occurring due to sudden anomalies, such as power losses or equipment failures, resulting in erroneous data being generated. Consequently, it is essential to incorporate strategies for distinguishing genuine anomalies from potential data corruption caused by faults. This paper presents algorithms capable of detecting such data corruption and incorporating the associated categorical information into the data reduction process. By utilizing these new features, the DRS system can effectively distinguish genuine anomalies from data that may have been corrupted by faults, such as power losses or equipment failures, and incorporate this information into the data reduction process. Using the WKB method, we analyze semiclassical calculations for the Hénon-Heiles system, specifically focusing on regions where classical motion is chaotic. Despite limitations of WKB approximations in areas with high amplitude fluctuations, they can provide accurate results for quantized action levels when restricted to steady-state motions. In the chaotic class of the vortex ring, our WKB calculations show significant agreement with exact molecular dynamics simulations, yielding precise quantization conditions and predicting the energy levels with notable accuracy. Moreover, our analysis reveals how WKB periodic action levels relate to the vortex ring class's instability and how this connection affects the distribution of energy levels. This relationship results in an intriguingly simple explanation for the statistical distribution of energy levels within this chaotic class, aligning with the predictions made by Berry and Tabor in their model involving a two-degree-of-freedom Hamiltonian Hamiltonian system. Our study further demonstrates that many of the features characteristic of regular chaotic classes can be demonstrated for a single, non-typical trajectory. This finding highlights the complexity of distinguishing regular from chaotic motion in chaotic trajectories and suggests that the definition of regular and chaotic motion may require a reevaluation in the context of semiclassical mechanics. This research is part of a broader investigation aimed at evaluating the validity and limitations of the WKB approximation in relation to Hamiltonian dynamics. Full molecular dynamics simulations validate our WKB calculations for quantized action levels when the amplitude of fluctuations in classical motion is below the WKB breakdown threshold. However, when this threshold is exceeded, significant deviations in quantized action levels are observed, accompanied by a loss of periodic motion in classical dynamics. In contrast, our WKB calculations continue to yield a comprehensive spectrum of quantized action levels, comprising both periodic and non-periodic motions. This outcome indicates that while the WKB approximation may capture regular behavior, its scope extends beyond this to include chaotic classes, such as the vortex ring regime discussed here. Consequently, this chaotic class effectively merges regular and chaotic domains, rendering the term "regular" in this context both misleading and irrelevant. As a result, we propose an alternative classification scheme that distinguishes three distinct domains within the vortex ring class based on the characteristics of classical motion: (1) periodic motion characterized by quasiperiodic motion in both the x and y directions, along with distinct energy subbands, (2) vortex ring flow with constant motion and distinct energy subbands and (3) chaotic motion featuring fluctuating motion in the x direction and an undulating motion in the y direction, along with overlapping energy levels.

With suitable modifications, this framework can be applied to forecast ICU demand among susceptible populations to inform public policy. This approach has the potential to enhance the overall effectiveness of COVID-19 mitigation strategies.  By prioritizing data processing speed and interpretability, we aim to motivate transformative research on machine learning in high-stakes, real-time decision-making scenarios. The task of visual relationship detection involves identifying connections between objects within an image and specifying the nature of these connections. A major challenge in this task lies in the vast possible relationships it can encompass, making traditional methods using handcrafted features ineffective. Recent successes in visual relationship detection have been achieved through the use of deep neural networks that first identify the objects within an image and then generate relationships between them, a approach that is difficult to optimize due to the vast possible relationships it can encompass, making traditional methods using handcrafted features ineffective. In this work, we introduce a sampling strategy, called balanced negative proposal sampling, that helps the model learn from its mistakes by first selecting proposals that are likely to be incorrect relationships and then sampling negative relationships that are similar to the proposed relationship, thus enabling the model to distinguish between actual relationships and negative ones. We test our sampling strategy on the Visual Relationship Detection task and demonstrate its effectiveness by achieving a significant improvement of 11.5% in mean Class Mean Average Precision (CMAP) on the LVISEval benchmark, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art method, VipCoco, by a margin of 2.5%. The success of action recognition systems is highly dependent on sufficient action data.  Given the high costs associated with manually labeling actions, it's essential to understand the impact of varying training dataset sizes on action recognition accuracy.  This study examines the implicit assumptions made by deep learning models when they generalize beyond their training data.  By analyzing the performance of a deep neural network on a action recognition task with gradually increasing training dataset sizes, we observed an intriguing phenomenon where the error rate initially decreases with each additional label, but eventually plateaus at a certain point.  This study also explores ways to enhance the implicit ability of deep models to generalize beyond their training data.  The proposed method for enhancing deep models involves an additional network that produces a soft, action-based attention vector in response to input video frames.  This attention vector is designed to focus on the action-relevant parts of the input stream and is trained using an end-to-end optimization algorithm.  Experimental results showed that the proposed method yielded significant performance improvements (up to 10%) over baseline models on the Kinetics-600 action recognition benchmark for training datasets of 1% and 5% of the total available data. The condition for the symmetry of the blow-up solution in the global case is determined by a specific configuration of the symmetry of the potential function Q(y). A corresponding description is given for the local case without Euclidean invariance. Additionally, an investigation of the local uniqueness of the blow-up solution is carried out, and requirements for the uniqueness are identified in terms of the potential function Q(y). If the symmetry of Q(y) is not completely determined, then the uniqueness depends on the specific configuration of its symmetry. A corresponding description is given for the over-determined case. A key component of our proof involves an energy decay estimate near the blow-up point, obtained through an energy integral formula and an energy optimization technique related to Moser-Trudinger inequality variants. This estimate produces a bound on the blow-up rate in the general case, and a sharper bound in the specific case where the symmetry of Q(y) is over-determined. Approximately a decade ago, neural network-based models for program generation began to take shape. Despite significant advancements, these models have struggled to match the precision achieved by static program analysis techniques in identifying program errors. Our research aims to bridge this gap by leveraging weak supervision from a static program analyzer to enhance a neural program generator. We've developed a method to use the analyzer's partial program corrections as training data, which has led to notable improvements in program quality. Our approach has two key components: first, identifying programs that require correction and collecting associated data from the static analyzer; second, incorporating the collected data into the neural generator through progressive refinement. Compared to a baseline model without correction data, our approach has shown a 12% increase in program precision and a 15% improvement in program quality as measured by mean squared error. Furthermore, our method has a key advantage of being model-agnostic, which means it can be applied to a broad range of neural program generators. Our research has a range of potential applications, which could be extended to scenarios where partial program corrections are available through testing and debugging techniques. The code for our research is openly accessible on GitHub at the specified URL.

Anomalous pattern detection in large, continuously updated datasets poses a challenging task for researchers. Current approaches typically focus on a single aspect, such as developing robust algorithms or utilizing multiple data sources, but fail to address the broader issues surrounding the generation and maintenance of such datasets. In contrast, our work introduces an incremental anomaly detection framework that gradually refines its predictions as it processes new data, without requiring a restart or significantly overhauling its underlying parameters. This approach leverages the benefits of parallel computing to analyze different data subgroups simultaneously, without experiencing performance degradation or difficulties in tuning parameters. The proposed method detects anomalies in each data subset effectively, even in the presence of curved decision boundaries and non-standard data distributions. The incremental nature of our algorithm allows it to excel in environments with rapidly evolving data distributions and frequent large data updates, as demonstrated by our evaluation results on both artificial and real-world datasets. Furthermore, our approach can be applied to a broad range of distribution types, as evidenced by its performance across 11 different dataset distributions in our experiments. The code for our algorithm is now available online. In addition to presenting our incremental anomaly detection algorithm, we also examine an associated problem involving anomaly feedback, although further research is needed to address this issue thoroughly. The problem of receiving new data based on previous anomaly detections poses an interesting problem that warrants exploration. The problem can be defined as follows: what new data is most likely to contain novel anomalies based on previously detected anomalies? This problem has significant practical implications, given the escalating costs associated with data collection and the increasing importance of anomaly detection in high-stakes applications, such as medical diagnosis and financial risk assessment. The problem also raises fundamental theoretical questions related to the relationship between new and existing anomalies, as well as the nature of continuous anomaly streams. The evaluation results for our incremental anomaly detection algorithm demonstrate its effectiveness in handling curved decision boundaries and non-standard data distributions. The algorithm achieved the lowest score in our experiments across multiple datasets, as measured by both precision and recall metrics. The experimental findings also validate our algorithm's incremental learning approach, as it consistently outperformed the standard batch learning approach across all datasets. The algorithm's parallel computing architecture was effective in handling different data subgroups simultaneously, as it consistently achieved comparable performance to the state-of-the-art batch algorithms while utilizing a fraction of the computational resources. The experimental results for our anomaly detection algorithm are visualized to illustrate its performance in relation to the data distribution. The algorithm's performance was evaluated in terms of precision and recall metrics across three distinct scenarios representing different data distributions.

A cryptographic scheme's deniability properties can be undermined if an authority can force a user to decrypt data, potentially infringing upon privacy rights. Conversely, a scheme enjoys future secrecy properties if there's no method an authority can employ to compel a user to reveal previously seen encrypted data. We investigate the relationship between these concepts and the principles of privacy and secrecy. Building upon existing research, we develop new notions for security and privacy in public-key encryption (PKE) schemes and PKE-based signatures (PKES), establishing deniability and future secrecy as inherent components of privacy and secrecy, respectively. To date, the only known constructions of public-key encryption and signature schemes featuring future secrecy properties rely on unfeasible computational tasks to achieve deniability. Consequently, our primary objective becomes identifying the feasibility of constructing public-key encryption and signature schemes with deniability. To this end, we present a class of public-key encryption schemes possessing future secrecy properties, tailored to provide weak security and flexibility in message space relationships. Building upon these schemes, we develop a framework enabling the conversion of any publicly retrievable one-time lockbox scheme into a publicly retrievable one-time lockbox scheme featuring deniability and future secrecy properties. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of our techniques to widely adopted public-key encryption and signature schemes, incorporating Fujisaki-Okamoto transforms and their variants. Our method for attaining security and privacy in public-key encryption schemes has far-reaching implications, given that all widely adopted public-key encryption schemes stem from a single basic construction, the one proposed by Fujisaki and Okamoto. In the realm of public-key signatures, our methodology complements previously accepted security standards set forth in the ISO/IEC 18033 series. Consequently, our techniques can be employed to enhance the security and privacy of existing public-key encryption and signature schemes, safeguarding user privacy rights protected by existing legislation. In the process, we introduce novel security definitions for public-key encryption and signature schemes, addressing future secrecy and computational overhead considerations. Ultimately, our research provides a framework for enhancing the security and privacy of public-key encryption and signature schemes, ensuring compliance with existing legislative privacy protections. In the process, we outline the development of publicly accessible tools for assessing and enhancing the security and privacy of public-key encryption and signature schemes. To assess the viability of different MDI-QKD implementations, our comprehensive analysis evaluates various protocols by measuring gains, error rates, and resulting key rates. We examine the characteristics of Cuckoo-QKD, a proposed variant that uses entangled source states with two distinct phases, and compare its performance to other MDI-QKD protocols. Through simulation, we find that Cuckoo-QKD outperforms other protocols, including the enhanced CV-QKD system, and demonstrate the potential for Cuckoo-QKD to achieve high key rates in the field. Furthermore, our findings indicate that Cuckoo-QKD's performance advantage holds even when considering the effects of channel loss, and suggest it may be resistant to certain attacks. However, our analysis also reveals that Cuckoo-QKD is susceptible to phase-rolling attacks, and therefore requires the implementation of adequate measures to ensure its security. As such, Cuckoo-QKD could serve as a relevant reference protocol for improving the performance of other MDI-QKD systems. Through code review and simulation, we make all relevant modifications and findings publicly accessible to facilitate further evaluation and improvement of Cuckoo-QKD. As well as offering security enhancements, our new MDI-QKD design goals prioritise minimal computational requirements, simple system configurations and low-cost implementation. For valued constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs), a fixed set of allowed constraints and a specific instance are given. The goal is to find a solution that minimizes the sum of user-defined values associated with each constraint. Specifically for Boolean minimization CSPs, the objective is to determine an assignment of variables that minimizes the sum of values corresponding to violated constraints. 

Previous research established the existence of a fully polynomial time approximation scheme (FPTAS) for solving general Boolean minimization CSPs, provided the number of variables is considered as the approximation factor. However, whether a PTAS exists for this problem has remained unclear. 

Our discovery addresses this question by demonstrating the existence of a PTAS for solving Boolean minimization CSPs with specific constraints, namely anti-anti constraints, for an arbitrary large number of variables. The algorithm's performance is directly proportional to the number of variables and can be applied to general Boolean CSPs by incorporating the use of dummy variables. Consequently, we can derive a PTAS for general Boolean CSPs with multiple variables per constraint. The algorithm's design involves the application of shifting-lattice aggrregate, a technique previously utilized in combinatorial optimization contexts. 

The implications of our invention are twofold. Firstly, it resolves the open question regarding the existence of PTAS for Boolean minimization CSPs with multiple variables per constraint. Secondly, it paves the way for further research into the development of approximation algorithms for non-Boolean minimization CSPs. 

In addition to the primary outcome, several auxiliary results have been derived. These include the existence of a PTAS for solving specific maximization CSPs and the application of our algorithm to design a PTAS for another specific problem. The design also leads to an interesting combinatorial theorem and may find relevant applications in other contexts. 

Finally, we outline several open questions and consider discussing the design in a more general framework.

Deep learning models excel at analyzing complex data and predicting various outcomes, but their lack of transparency complicates the auditing process and risk assessment. To address this issue, the XAI framework focuses on making AI systems more understandable and trustworthy. However, the current approach to XAI is often criticized for prioritizing regulatory compliance over best practices in data analysis. In response, this study leverages the XAI methodology within the context of medical image analysis to evaluate the performance of deep learning models. Specifically, it investigates the impact of feature importance visualizations on model performance, relying on real-world clinical data. The findings indicate that selecting input images with high importance scores can significantly improve model accuracy and reliability. Moreover, models trained on these carefully curated subsets of data exhibit better performance compared to traditional training methods. Ultimately, this study demonstrates the value of combining XAI techniques and rigorous data analysis to develop more effective and reliable deep learning models for medical image analysis. Experimental results validate the approach, revealing that models performed better and produced more accurate predictions when trained on carefully selected datasets. Nonetheless, further research is required to fully realize the potential of XAI in medical image analysis. In conclusion, this study showcases a data-driven strategy for enhancing the performance of deep learning models through the careful selection of input images, emphasizing the importance of combining XAI and data analysis expertise. The associated code is publicly accessible for replication purposes. The underlying dataset is part of the CAD-THOR challenge and consists of 5000 annotated video game images depicting various surgical tasks. KIC 9267654, a small A-type main-sequence star, exhibits an unusual rotational profile that was initially reported. This profile shows a significant slow-down in the star's middle section. Possible explanations for this phenomenon could be various stellar phenomena or a possible binary star system. To further investigate, we collected high-cadence, short cadence, and light curve data from the Kepler spacecraft, as well as spectroscopic data from the HARPS and AMBER instruments. Analyzing the data revealed that KIC 9267654 is actually a binary star system consisting of a 1.53-solar-mass primary star and a 1.11-solar-mass secondary star. Although the binary system orbits the primary star in a relatively close orbit, the stars do not overlap. Due to the binary system, the primary star's rotation profile exhibits an irregular pattern as the secondary star synchronizes its orbit with the primary star's rotation. As they rotate in harmony, the primary star's rotation profile displays slow and fast areas, ultimately leading to an irregular rotation profile. Notably, the binary system's behavior is comparable to that of the HR 9284 system, which features a similar primary star rotation profile. Furthermore, our analysis revealed the binary system's orbital period is approximately 19.56 days and the secondary star's mass is approximately 0.511 solar masses. In addition, we determined the stars' relative velocities and found the primary star is spinning relatively slowly with a velocity of approximately 64 km/s, while the secondary star has a velocity of approximately 189 km/s. As a result, the primary star's middle section has slowed down due to the gravitational interaction with the faster-spinning secondary star, leading to an unusual rotation profile. Ultimately, our analysis confirmed the binary nature of the star system and explained the underlying cause of KIC 9267654's unusual rotation profile. However, our research did not uncover sufficient evidence to support the existence of a third body in the star system. Lastly, we estimated the star system's age to be approximately 200 million years based on its color and the evolution of the binary system. Consequently, KIC 9267654 is the second known binary star system featuring an externally synchronized primary star with an irregular rotation profile. As a result, this star system offers an excellent opportunity for scientists to study the effects of external torques on a primary star's rotation profile. Previous studies on age of information (AoI) have primarily focused on individual systems, whether they were discrete or continuous time based. This study seeks to compare the stationary AoI distribution of these time frameworks and explore the implications on a dual-server setup where two servers, one operating in each time framework, update a single queue. We establish the normal and phased closed queueing systems' stationary AoI distributions for discrete and continuous time systems and analyze the interplay between these time frameworks. Numerical calculations are presented to illustrate the effectiveness of this study's findings. Notably, this study reveals that discrete time systems tend to have older AoI values compared to continuous time systems, with the former exhibiting increased variance. This disparity in AoI distributions influences the dual-server setup, resulting in a discrete time system's update interval being generally shorter than its continuous time counterpart, despite the former's older AoI values. Consequently, the stationary AoI distribution of discrete time systems is outperformed, albeit marginally, by that of continuous time systems in the phased closed queueing system. We examine how Drinfeld twists are affected under base change in a Drinfeld's correspondence for function fields. Admissible Drinfeld twists are examined in both the classical and quantum settings, finding that specific constraints must be met; these settings also allow us to establish correspondence between isomorphism classes of Drinfeld twists and divisors. Additionally, we develop a fully faithful functor from the category of Drinfeld twists to the category of divisors based on the Mumford formula, and demonstrate that this functor extends to a fully faithful embedding of the category of Drinfeld twists into the category of line bundles on divisors, with line bundles represented by Drinfeld twists having a particular property. This enables us to establish a one-to-one correspondence between isomorphism classes of line bundles with this property and divisors. Furthermore, we introduce the notion of admissible Drinfeld twists in the algebraic context and show they behave correctly under base change, leading to a fully faithful functor from the category of admissible Drinfeld twists to the category of divisors. Finally, we introduce quantum admissible Drinfeld twists and show they correspond to quantum divisors in a specific representation.

Our study provides critical insights into understanding the complex behavior of helium nanodots in silicon crystal lattices.

We examine the relationship between quantum nonlocality in multipartite systems and their correlation-based context, known as correlation complexity. Specifically, we investigate strong quantum nonlocality in multipartite systems in relation to their unextendible product bases. Initially, a global state is shown to display strong quantum nonlocality if and only if at least one of its unextendible product bases consists of highly complex correlations. We establish specific identities concerning the absolute values of degenerate Eisenstein series on Weyl group cosets, which involve specific Weyl group elements and character values. These identities enable us to derive formulas for computing the norms of degenerate Eisenstein series and relate them to Weyl group cosets. Additionally, we obtain expressions for computing the norms in a specific context where the Weyl group has a non-trivial action on the set of roots. Multiple computational models of the central nervous system have been developed, leading to a call for a unifying framework that can effectively utilize these models to address pressing medical issues, such as finding the cause of Parkinson's Disease. This paper proposes a general approach to incorporate various neuroinformatics tools and apply them to Parkinson's research. By leveraging existing models and incorporating new data, a neural network can learn relationships between them, ultimately enabling the identification of Parkinson's-related alterations in computational brain simulations. This approach was demonstrated using LFP recordings from a rodent model of Parkinson's Disease, resulting in a network that can distinguish between healthy and diseased brain patterns. One key feature extracted from this approach pinpointed a specific brain area affected in the model. This area is comparable to the substantia nigra pars compacta, a key component of basal ganglia affected by Parkinson's Disease, suggesting that this approach may lead to new insights into the disease's cause and could potentially inform the design of neuroprosthetic devices targeting this area. Furthermore, this approach may be applied to other complex diseases and help bridge the gap between computational neuroscience and clinical research. Recent findings suggest that AGN-driven outflows play a crucial role in the co-evolution of galaxies and supermassive black holes (SMBHs), which could explain the connection between the growth of SMBHs and their host galaxies. To maintain the necessary momentum to impact galaxies, these outflows must originate from a highly energetic AGN. By examining a large sample of 179 AGNs with estimated masses of $10^{8.5}$ < M$_{ \rm SMBH}$$ < 10^{10.5} M_{\odot}$ based on their AGN-driven outflow measurements, this study finds that more massive SMBHs are found in galaxies with higher rates of star formation, but only when considering local density environments. When adjusting for central density, these relations become linear. This possible non-linear relationship around $M_{\rm SMBH} = 10^{9.2} M_{\odot}$ may indicate a transition in the growth mode of SMBHs. A linear relationship holds between galaxy pairs, suggesting that equal mass matter is transferred during mergers. Upcoming surveys with large spectroscopic databases will allow for a deeper examination of this potential SMBH merger phase transition and its implications for the co-evolution of galaxies and SMBHs. Until then, this study provides key observational evidence for a significant SMBH merger phase transition around $M_{\rm SMBH} = 10^{9.2} M_{\odot}$. Although viewport prediction frameworks have shown promise in various scenarios, our research reveals a notable shortcoming: they tend to misestimate the content within the viewer's field of view when encountering spoken text. To address this limitation, we propose incorporating video subtitles into the prediction model by leveraging the established layout and style of subtitles as a visual scheme. By doing so, we've developed a neural network that learns to anticipate the viewer's viewport based on video subtitles and learned layout preferences, resulting in a 14.8% reduction in viewport prediction errors compared to the baseline approach. Experimental results indicate that our approach achieves a precision of 0.73 and a recall of 0.75 in evaluating viewport prediction accuracy, outperforming alternative solutions that rely on viewer data and eye movement patterns. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our model's ability to anticipate the viewer's viewport is enhanced when presented with spoken text in a more visually appealing format, resembling the layout of subtitles in video content. Additionally, we present a qualitative analysis of the predicted viewports in relation to speech content and optical flow maps, indicating that our approach can effectively anticipate the viewer's eye movements even in the absence of actual eye movement data. Consequently, our proposed system can contribute to the development of more immersive video experiences that adapt to individual viewer preferences. The code for this research is available online.

By creating a hierarchy of PEPOs, we increase the bond dimension requirement from $x$ to $x^2$ in the next level down, ultimately approximating thermal states and time evolution within the context of AFM Hamiltonians. We discover that, in contrast to typical PEPO construction, the bond dimension requirement is directly proportional to the system size for this specific class of Hamiltonians. This newfound understanding enables us to derive an upper limit on the accuracy of approximations, finding that it is capped at $O(1/\text{sys. size})$. We demonstrate how this framework eradicates the growth of computational cost when approximating thermal states and time evolution, utilizing the $XX$ chain as an example. We also establish that our method surpasses previously proposed PEPO approximation techniques in terms of fidelity. Furthermore, we utilize this hierarchy to construct a series of PEPOs that yield an ensemble of hierarchies, each corresponding to distinct photon frequencies, thereby approximating thermal states and time evolution for these scenarios. We observe that our proposed hierarchy serves as an optimal minimally entangled benchmark when the number of spins is extremely low, thereby serving as a baseline against which other proposals can be evaluated in terms of their accuracy. Lastly, we anticipate that our method to mitigate computational cost will be applicable across a broad spectrum of Hamiltonian systems. We demonstrate that subtle variations in the motion of certain active dimers can be greatly amplified when interacting with an external potential, reminiscent of how a steering wheel influences the motion of vehicles. This phenomenon enables dimers to navigate complex navigation tasks. Although this technique is exceptional and only applicable in specific environments, it opens up possibilities for developing more complex and efficient navigation strategies in environments where our method can be applied locally. Additionally, we find that our approach can be used in scenarios where both type-A and type-B particles are present. Furthermore, we propose a related concept of'motion amplification' as a universal framework that can be applied beyond active dimers and provide examples of its relevance in other situations. Leveraging this framework, we modulate the motion of active triomers by exploiting asymmetries in their dynamics. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of how motion can be controlled in active particle systems and may have implications for designing efficient strategies of propulsion and navigation in microscopic systems.

When the number of covers is limited to 1 and k is 2, we determined the problem to be solvable via an exponential-time algorithm, which has a time complexity of O(n^k * n^2). When k is 2 and an exponential-time algorithm is allowed, we further found it to be solvable by utilizing a strong shortest path approach, resulting in a time complexity of O(n^4). If the graph is known to be free from positive weights and k is 2, we established a time complexity of O(n^3). Finally, we demonstrated that a time complexity of O(n^3) is optimal for the general weighted graph case when k is 2, as it is a known problem that requires at least an O(n^3) time complexity when using a non-deterministic Turing machine.
