This research investigates the development of variable stepsize Stochastic Generalized Linear Models (SGLMs) for approximating expectations under the assumption of randomly changing model parameters. We demonstrate that traditional, fixed-stepsize Model Selection methods and Generalized Linear Models can be viewed as special cases of our Variable Stepsize SGLM framework. However, their performance is impaired by model misalignment. In contrast, our experiments show that our approach yields superior results, particularly when modeled using nonuniform time intervals, rather than uniform intervals. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that our Variable Stepsize SGLM can process time series data at a significantly lower computational cost compared to methods based on Model Selection. We also establish an essential condition for the convergence of our estimator and provide an alternative expression for the error covariance matrix. Additionally, our research finds that our method's performance is optimal in terms of minimax theory and that our algorithm can be modified to accommodate missing data observations. We also evaluate our approach using synthetic data and real-world examples from the areas of population growth, disease spread, and stock price analysis. All implementation details are outlined in the appendices, along with a discussion on potential applications and future directions.

Recent studies demonstrate that deep-learning models can be sensitive to small changes in their parameters and become unstable when scaled up for important applications like evaluating student essays.
This paper delves into the reasons behind the poor performance of these models on assessment tasks and proposes a simple solution to address two significant issues: oversensitivity and unstability.
A data augmentation technique is outlined to enhance the robustness of these models, along with a straightforward modification to their learning algorithm to minimize the impact of stochastic aspects.
The proposed method is then applied to an automatic essay scoring task, where a deep neural network that was trained and fine-tuned with data augmentation outperformed other baseline models, including one that used generative adversarial networks.
Notably, this model demonstrated improved robustness and stability, producing consistent scores for the same essays and avoiding extreme variations due to minor changes in its parameters.
Overall, the research indicates that deep neural networks can achieve high accuracy on complex tasks like evaluating student essays, both reliably and consistently, with minimal instability or bias.

This study investigates how entomopathogenic nematodes influence the dynamics of an insect population under different reproductive modes and density-dependent predation patterns. We analyzed the impact of adding the nematodes as a biological control method, examining population responses to different levels of infection and predation intensity. Our mathematical model reveals that increasing infection severity leads to a decline in population birth rates and ultimately contributes to reduced population sizes. However, the model also shows that intense predation can counteract the effect of the nematodes, potentially even triggering an increase in populations if predation is heavily density-dependent. Our findings suggest that biological control using entomopathogenic nematodes may be most effective in environments where water is scarce, likely because these conditions favor the development of the nematodes' infectious stages. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that the nematodes could provide sustained birth control, reducing the target population's size below a critically low threshold through which it can recover on its own. This could provide a basis for developing more effective biological control methods that combine the nematodes with other management techniques. Overall, our research demonstrates that entomopathogenic nematodes can serve as a viable biological control tool, particularly when used in water-scarce environments and perhaps in conjunction with other population regulation methods. The model we present can be applied to various host-parasite systems characterized by direct tissue damage caused by the nematodes and their density-dependent regulation. The theoretical model we developed also includes a biological control scenario in which the nematodes lower the target population's birth rate below a critically low threshold, enabling population recovery on its own. The model's applicability and biological relevance are further supported by a companion field study reported elsewhere. The model's unique aspect lies in its analysis of the interactions between the nematodes' infection stages and their host, an aspect that has not been extensively explored in the literature. Nevertheless, our model suggests that this could vary depending on the virus strain and host parameters, and that in other cases, necroptosis might actually help contain the infection's spread. Furthermore, we propose that the current pandemic surge could be attributed to the prevalence of necroptotic cells in infected individuals, and that in the late stages of the pandemic, apoptosis-dominated cell mortality patterns might contribute to a decline in virus spread. This research presents HELMHOLTZ, a verification tool developed for Michelson code used in Tezos, a public blockchain platform. TEZOS' scripting language, Michelson, enables the creation of smart contracts and validates transactions. However, Michelson's complexity poses verification challenges. Building upon existing research, the HELMHOLTZ framework expands the capabilities of verifications by introducing a new approach to analyze Michelson programs in a step-by-step manner. This leads to significant performance improvements and efficient verification of contract properties. Furthermore, the team behind this research successfully applied the HELMHOLTZ framework to verify multiple smart contracts, including the Tezos social governance contract. Additionally, the framework includes a graphical user interface that facilitates interaction with Michelson code and contract verifications. Nevertheless, the development faces a crucial limitation as the ANS() Michelson function remains unanalysed. Consequently, the team is seeking enhancements to overcome this constraint. The HELMHOLTZ framework consists of approximately 3000 lines of code and is openly accessible on GitHub. Elastography, a technique that leverages elastography algorithms and ultrasound technology to map tissue stiffness, has faced challenges in recent years. Elastography algorithms require precise displacement measurements in the axial and lateral directions; however, previous studies have demonstrated that axial displacement estimation is significantly more accurate than lateral displacement estimation. To address this issue, researchers have proposed various methods to enhance lateral displacement estimation, including the use of elastography algorithms that integrate information from successive ultrasound frames. While these methods have shown some promise, they are often hampered by high computational complexity, require additional equipment, or fail to account for speckle patterns in ultrasound images. To address these limitations, the authors introduce the localized gradient operator (LGO), a simple and efficient method that estimates local gradient values to enhance lateral displacement estimation. The LGO method utilizes a weighted sum of absolute differences between speckle patterns in ultrasound images and is designed to minimize side effects from adjacent pixels. When tested on a dataset consisting of 50 elastography samples, the LGO method demonstrated a significant reduction in displacement error (from 12.57 to 8.76) when compared to the conventional method, indicating that the LGO method can be an effective and efficient solution for enhancing lateral displacement estimation. The source code for the LGO method is available online for review and potential collaboration. To further improve the method, suggestions for future work include applying the LGO algorithm to magnetic resonance elastography and utilizing deep learning techniques to enhance its performance. The authors also propose integrating the LGO method with axial displacement estimation algorithms to develop a comprehensive elastography framework. Most programming languages' reference materials utilize logical pseudocodes to illustrate their language principles, however, these pseudocodes frequently disregard fundamental guidelines, resulting in inaccurate and potentially hazardous examples that confuse learners and confuse those who attempt to translate them into actual code. In contrast, logical pseudocodes are crafted with precision and emphasis on safety, these pseudocodes are designed to serve as specifications for static program analysis tools and must adhere to key properties including terminability, detectability of errors, safety, and predictability. The primary goal of this study is to demonstrate that many widely-used programming languages' reference materials contain incorrect examples which contradict the safety properties required of logical pseudocodes. The findings are demonstrated through examples taken from renowned textbooks and official language documentation. Furthermore, this study proposes a framework for upgrading these examples to compliant logical pseudocodes, thereby making them suitable as specifications for static program analysis tools. The proposed framework is exemplified through concrete code modifications and format transformations. The primary benefits of this study are twofold: Firstly, it provides precise examples of programming concepts through accurate and safe pseudocodes, thereby enriching programming education; Secondly, this study offers a range of compliant examples and corresponding invalid counter-examples, thereby empowering the development of advanced learning tools that leverage program analysis algorithms to educate programmers about complex topics, mistake identification, and program improvement. The simplest form of this type of learning technology is a static program verification tool that is integrated with a counter-example visualization, a feature that is absent in existing educational code review tools. This study also proposes a suite of programming education materials that are designed to evaluate the effectiveness of this type of learning technology in various educational settings. The proposed technology and learning materials are demonstrated through a concrete prototype that utilizes the SpiderMonkey JavaScript engine and the Marionette automation framework. The results from the empirical evaluation of this prototype in real-world classroom environments indicate a significant improvement in student understanding, error detection, and programming safety. The proposed technology and learning materials also facilitate the automatic production of valid and safe programming examples, thereby enriching programming education by providing accurate and safe pseudocodes that illustrate programming concepts. This study is an extension to the use of adaptive instance normalization layers in cycleGANs, specifically addressing the limitation of this approach being confined to two-domain applications. We explore the adaptability of cycleGANs that incorporate AdaIN layers in three distinct scenarios: targeting a single target domain, multiple target domains, and the scenario where the source domain is unknown. Our research demonstrates that incorporating AdaIN layers significantly enhances the performance of cycleGANs across all evaluated scenarios, even outperforming the baseline cycleGAN model in two-domain settings. Moreover, our method's ability to utilize guidance from multiple target domains leads to state-of-the-art results on the birds-to-aircraft transfer task. The proposed approach also facilitates the development of cycleGANs that are interpretable and robust to unexpected input images. The source code and model weights are available for download at https://github.com/ruikou/AdaIN-CycleGANs.

We suggest a framework called Multi-Aspect Dialog Language Model that not only enhances dialog representation learning but also offers a straightforward way to build high-quality multi-view models. Unlike conventional score functions that are calculated using unidirectional contexts, the proposed model employs a multi-view score function that considers contexts from multiple angles. This approach enables us to derive a method for unsupervised multi-view dialog representation learning by introducing a novel grouping objective that aims to cluster embeddings with the same topic based on buyer product information. Unlike conventional methods that typically employ supervised training and score functions that only account for single aspects, our proposed model can automatically extract multiple aspects from context and assign weights to them, outperforming state-of-the-art models that use context and learned features for dialog modification classification. Experimental results show that the proposed model achieves comparable performance when supervised and significantly outperforms other unsupervised multi-view models. Moreover, an analysis of the extracted dialog aspects confirms their relevance to the shopping context. Additionally, we observed improved performance when supervised but found that the model struggled to extract distinct aspects from unsupervised data. In order to facilitate the development of public datasets for multi-aspect dialog language models, we released a newly created dataset called AntiShopping that includes dialog data recorded with buyers attempting to persuade others to buy products in public and features labeled aspect spans. The concept of deformed halo rotors poses a challenging problem for contemporary nuclear theory. To tackle this issue, our research employs a novel computational approach that uses a deformed harmonic oscillator potential to model rotating nuclei. Within this framework, we investigate a range of rotating nuclei, including isotopes with deformed halos, such as $^{42}$Mg and $^{72}$Zr, as well as others with deformed shapes, such as $^{162}$Er and $^{182}$Os. By comparing the calculated density distributions to experimental data, we find that only considerations of deformed initial conditions can accurately reproduce observed shapes of account for configuration effects on rotational states. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the densities of rotating nuclei become prolate at low-spin states due to collective correlations, whereas high-spin states or those with deformed shapes maintain their original shapes. The calculated density distributions are also compared with Monte Carlo shell model calculations to validate our approach. Additionally, we analyze the moments of inertia and B(E2) transition probabilities to assess the performance of our method. Our study demonstrates that computational simulations utilizing deformed harmonic oscillator bases can effectively simulate rotating nuclei undergoing shape transitions or existing in deformed equilibrium states. However, at intermediate spins or in systems with multiple-proton or -neutron configurations, more advanced approaches, such as the Monte Carlo shell model, may be required to accurately account for correlations between different rotational bands. Nevertheless, this computational approach may prove useful for constructing wave functions for studies of high-energy physics or very heavy rotating nuclei. We examine the Tsallis distribution through the lens of social dynamics, drawing inspiration from bail jumpers' risk preferences as studied by Yang and Patacchini (2019). Building on their findings, we model Tsallis entropy as a measure of diversity within a social system, even if the underlying population is not directly observable. This approach enables us to explore general properties of the Tsallis distribution in relation to social dynamics, as well as assess the applicability of Tsallis entropy to capture diversity in a broad sense, given that it can be utilized as an alternative means of quantifying diversity relative to specified functions. Moreover, we find that Tsallis entropy can be interpreted in the context of weighted differences between moments, potentially facilitating its utilization in analyzing skewed data distributions. In the process, we clarify the distinctions between Tsallis and other entropy types, such as Shannon and Lin-Ni entropy, which can also be viewed as quantifying diversity according to distinct criteria. As a result, our analysis offers Tsallis entropy a fresh perspective, one that positions it as a viable method for measuring the diversity present within social systems, even if the underlying population is not directly observable. This perspective is further illustrated by exploring the relationships between Tsallis entropy and the bail jumpers' risk preferences as modeled by Yang and Patacchini (2019). Our analysis also reveals that Tsallis entropy can be viewed as an alternative means of quantifying the disparity between different groups within a society, thereby making it a potentially useful tool for conducting social inequality research. In conclusion, this paper clarifies the applicability of Tsallis entropy in capturing the complexity of social systems, even if the underlying population is not directly observable, as evidenced by its applicability to analyzing skewed data distributions and its ability to quantify diversity relative to specified functions. As such, it can be utilized as an accessible measure of Tsallis entropy in a broad sense, making it an integral part of our ongoing research initiative. This work is part of our broader research project that is openly available at https://github.com/ajw85/Tsallis-Social-Dynamics. This document summarizes our research findings and provides a comprehensive overview of the related theory and methodology. It is intended for a diverse audience with an interest in social dynamics, entropy types, and the underlying mathematics, as well as potential users of our research. Hybrid quantum classical (HQC) methods integrate quantum mechanics with molecular dynamics, offering an efficient approach for computing molecular properties. However, determining the Hamiltonian operator is crucial for these methods. In this research, we establish a new strategy to derive the Hamiltonian operator from quantum equilibrium states, specifically for systems that reach a stationary quantum state. This approach is valid for four types of Hamiltonian dynamics: microcanonical, canonical, grand canonical, and quantum equilibrium states. We demonstrate that the expected energy can be computed directly from the quantum equilibrium distribution. By applying this method to harmonic oscillators and diatomic molecules, we show that the expected energy matches the total energy for specific Hamiltonian dynamics. In contrast, energy discrepancies arise in other scenarios. Finally, we illustrate that the expected energy can be used to update the Hamiltonian operator in molecular dynamics simulations. According to our results, using expected energies instead of instantaneous energy could lead to more efficient and convergent HQC simulations. To achieve this, we propose modifying the Hamiltonian operator in accordance with the predicted energies, yielding an intriguing novel HQC approach. This innovative protocol may prove beneficial for a broad range of molecular chemistry applications.

This approach begins with detecting the adenomas on endoscopic videos using a network that is trained and refined, allowing for the identification of multiple adenomas within a single frame. Once detected, a convolutional neural network is used to classify and grade the adenomas based on their morphology, resulting in accurate results according to clinical standards. What's unique about this method is that it distinguishes itself from other approaches by handling multiple objects of interest, making it suitable for analyzing videos that contain numerous adenomas. What's more, this algorithm can operate in real-time, making it suitable for real-world applications where timely processing is essential. Speech-to-text systems typically rely on large datasets of aligned text and speech segments, but building such datasets in low-resource languages is challenging due to high production costs and limited data availability. Recent advances in zero-shot speech translation, which enable translation without direct data alignment, show promising results but are limited by the need for pre-training speech and text models. This paper delves deeper into improving zero-shot speech translation, specifically for models that do not rely on cross-domain pre-training. We evaluate two approaches to fine-tune the models: first, modifying the zero-shot framework's frame-level alignment model to account for sentence-level structure, and second, expanding the training data to include sentences that are likely to be generated as translations. This is achieved by using contrastive loss on generated sentences in a low-dimensional space. We further explore an alternative method of expanding the training data by generating additional data based on the available transcripts. Our methods significantly enhance performance in few-shot settings and outperform baseline methods across multiple speech-to-text datasets, showcasing the effectiveness of improving the alignment model's sentence-level performance and expanding the training data to include generated sentences. This has a more notable impact when expanding the data is possible, with a notable exception of the challenging CSTR dataset. This correspondence enables us to derive a simplified and intuitive form of the Harish-Chandra isomorphism. We further leverage this understanding to derive explicit formulas for characters of mixed bosonic and fermionic representations through their connections to Schur elements and shifted Schur polynomials. These formulas provide a direct link between the geometry of Schur varieties and representation theory. We also introduce a new basis for the algebra U(s0), which reflects its decomposition in terms of shifted Schur polynomials. A novel concept, local spin-orbit coupling, is introduced to describe the behavior of transition metal oxides. It accounts for interaction effects and local distortions within the spin-orbit coupling framework. This idea is applied to understand magnetoelectric behavior in ferroelectric antiferromagnets. In particular, a specific material, iron-doped magnesium manganite, is analyzed using a local spin-orbit coupling model that shows that the highest d-orbital with the largest positive spin-orbit coupling can be stabilized through competition with crystal field splitting and neighboring interaction effects. This leads to the generation of magnetic dipole fields that interact with the electric field of the crystal, facilitating magnetoelectric coupling. Local spin-orbit coupling is then linked to the free energy of the system, enabling the prediction of magnetic domain wall arrangements that influence magnetoelectric behavior. Finally, this theory is validated through comparison with existing data and predictions, followed by suggestions for experimental verification of the proposed local spin-orbit coupling framework. Experimental evidence supporting this theory can be sought through magnetic domain wall width and magnetoelectric coupling constant measurements as a function of iron concentration and temperature. Additionally, the ability to describe ground state magnetic structures and the energy associated with magnetic domain walls using the local spin-orbit coupling model lays the foundation for further investigations into the fundamental aspects of magnetism in complex metals and compounds. This study highlights the potential of local spin-orbit coupling to unify disparate phenomena, such as magnetoelectric coupling, multiferroicity, and heavy-electron magnetism, that are characterized by strong spin-orbit coupling and competing orders. Moreover, understanding local spin-orbit coupling is crucial for designing materials with tailored spin-orbit coupling and magnetic properties, an essential step towards the development of novel spin-orbit coupled states of matter. This vision is supported by several proposals for experimental investigations that aim to directly manipulate local spin-orbit coupling and study its effects in various systems. Ultimately, local spin-orbit coupling is an emergent concept that offers a path toward a new paradigm in the design of materials with exotic spin properties. This new approach not only empowers the creation of materials with tailored spin properties but may also pave the way for fundamental breakthroughs in our comprehension of correlated electrons and strong interactions. We establish a relationship between the relative $I$-functions of toric complete intersections with smooth divisors, specifically expressing one in terms of the others. Furthermore, this relationship involves a regular holonomic module and its deep learning-inspired representation. By applying this connection, we can determine the dimension of the space involving relative $I$-functions. Moreover, this approach outperforms previous methods for certain parameters. Finally, we illustrate our findings by examining an example of a non-toric complete intersection. This research generalizes our earlier studies on hyperplane arrangements and pseudodifferential operators. It also connects to a broader framework of hypergeometric functions and special holonomic modules. Notably, this relationship can be viewed as an extension of the Gauss-Manin connection to the level of $I$-functions. We also derive an explicit formula for relative zeta functions. This work is in line with our program of exploring mathematical structures inspired by physics and deep learning and aims to provide a foundation for further research on learning algorithms using non-holonomic modules.

Advanced data visualization is crucial for data analysis, particularly in dimensions higher than three. Many interactive visualization tools are often part of data analysis platforms, but they require substantial user expertise. We present ViDaExpert, an intuitive web-based application for visualizing high-dimensional data. It offers three primary functions: (1) automatic selection of the most distinctive features in data, (2) visualization of multidimensional data in a user-friendly way, and (3) exploration of how data points are correlated. We demonstrate ViDaExpert's benefits through a real-world application involving the analysis of email spam data. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive evaluation of ViDaExpert's performance using a range of synthetic datasets. The system's code, data used in evaluations, and user instructions are available at https://github.com/compmeta/ViDaExpert. We also invite users to try ViDaExpert at https://vida.expert. We plan to enhance ViDaExpert by incorporating more features and appealing visuals in future developments. The system's code can be utilized to build similar applications utilizing D3.js libraries. We also intend to explore various correlation analysis techniques and integrate them into ViDaExpert in due course. We believe ViDaExpert can be a useful tool for researchers who need to analyze high-dimensional data in their studies. We would appreciate feedback from users to aid in the ongoing enhancement of the system. ViDaExpert was built using R Shiny for the main application and Rely for the correlation analysis, with D3.js libraries for visualizations and Plotly for additional plots. It can be run locally with R Shiny or accessed online at https://vida.expert. We have made the code for the application, data employed in evaluations, and a user manual available at https://github.com/compmeta/ViDaExpert. We invite potential users to test and offer feedback on ViDaExpert at https://vida.expert. We intend to build upon this initial iteration of ViDaExpert in future projects. We wish to express our gratitude to the creators of multiple open-source projects whose code we have utilized in developing this application. We look forward to collaborating with data analysis communities to aid in the ongoing development of ViDaExpert. We are confident that this application has the potential to contribute positively to various data-driven research projects. This research focuses on developing a direct method for high-order approximations of functions within mesh elements, specifically addressing polynomials in two dimensions. The proposed technique involves creating a two-dimensional monomial-based interpolation function with an elevated degree of accuracy, which can be applied to more complex functions like the Poisson equation. Initially, a high-order one-dimensional interpolation function can be constructed using non-uniform data points. Building upon this, a two-dimensional interpolation function is developed with a similar level of accuracy, determined by the number of data points in each direction. Several numerical experiments demonstrate the technique's performance, including situations where the interpolation function is directly applied and others where it serves as a precursor to an indirect approximation using FEM. The results show that using a higher-order two-dimensional interpolation function can significantly enhance the accuracy of the approximation, with an apparent advantage when compared to FEM under certain conditions. Furthermore, the technique is susceptible to the 'pollution' effect when using low-order one-dimensional interpolation functions, while it can yield precise approximations when employing high-order variants. The proposed method also demonstrates comparable efficiency to FEM in terms of computational cost. Lastly, solving a mass-conservation equation demonstrated the technique's ability to maintain accuracy in the presence of smooth updates to the solution. The technique's potential applications include utilizing high-order FEM data as input to the direct approximation method, which could be particularly useful for solving PDEs with disparate solution components. The technique also offers a standalone alternative to FEM. The implementation of the proposed method has been made available as a Python package, enabling easy integration of high-order approximations into existing codes. The package can be employed to directly generate high-order approximations over mesh elements or to create interpolants for mapping data from one dimension to another. The most effective approach, in terms of accuracy and computational cost, is identified as using an identical level of accuracy in both directions, resulting in significantly higher accuracy with only marginally higher computational cost when compared to low-order variants. The technique offers an appealing alternative to FEM, particularly when high-order elements are employed. The proposed method has the potential to be further improved, with possibilities including the incorporation of coefficient approximation and the integration of least squares projection methods. The research also paves the way for exploring high-order approximations of functions over mesh elements using data points derived from the solution of the PDE itself.
